title: The Woman Who Found Radium
text:
When Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw in 1867, Poland was not a free country. Russia ruled the city, and Polish children had to learn in Russian at school. Girls had another problem too: they could not go to university. So Maria and her sister joined a secret school that moved from house to house. The teachers changed the place every week, and the police never found it.

The two sisters made a plan. First, Maria would work and send money to Paris, where her sister Bronisława wanted to study medicine. Later, her sister would help her in return. For about six years, Maria worked as a teacher in a family's home in the countryside. In the evenings she read physics and chemistry books alone.

In 1891 she finally went to Paris and started at the Sorbonne. She lived in a small, cold room and often forgot to eat. In winter she wore all her clothes in bed to stay warm. But she worked very hard, and she finished first in her class in physics. In Paris she also changed her name to Marie.

In 1894 she met Pierre Curie, a quiet scientist who studied crystals and magnets. They shared the same love of science, and they married in 1895. For their honeymoon they rode bicycles around the French countryside.

At that time, a French scientist named Henri Becquerel had found that uranium gave off strange, invisible rays. The young scientist wanted to understand these rays. She measured them very carefully and saw that they came from the atoms themselves. She called this new effect "radioactivity", a word we still use today.

Working with Pierre in an old, cold shed, she found two new elements in 1898. She named the first one polonium, after her home country, Poland. The second one was radium, which glowed softly in the dark. To get a tiny amount of pure radium, the couple had to work with tonnes of rock for several years.

In 1903, Marie, Pierre and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Three years later, a terrible accident happened. Her husband was hit by a horse-drawn cart in a Paris street and died. She was heartbroken, but she continued their work. She took his job at the university and became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry.

When the First World War began, she wanted to help. She put X-ray machines into cars and drove them to the front herself, so doctors could find bullets inside wounded soldiers. People called these cars "little Curies". She also trained women to use the machines.

Nobody knew at that time how dangerous radioactivity was. She often carried radium in her pocket. She died in 1934, probably because of the radiation. Even today, her notebooks are still radioactive, and they are kept in special boxes. Visitors who want to read them must wear protective clothing.

questions.q: How did Maria pay for her studies in Paris?
options: She won a prize from the Russian government.
Her sister helped her after Maria first worked and helped her sister.
Pierre Curie paid for her room.
She sold radium to doctors.
questions.explain: Metne göre iki kız kardeş bir plan yaptı: önce Maria çalışıp Bronisława'ya para gönderdi, sonra ablası ona yardım etti. Doğru cevap "Her sister helped her after Maria first worked and helped her sister."

questions.q: Why are Marie Curie's notebooks kept in special boxes today?
options: They are very old and easy to break.
They are written in a secret language.
They are still radioactive.
They belong to the Polish government.
questions.explain: Son paragrafta defterlerin hâlâ radyoaktif olduğu, bu yüzden özel kutularda saklandığı söyleniyor: "They are still radioactive."

title: Sinan, the Builder of Domes
text:
If you walk around Istanbul, you will see his work almost everywhere. Mosques, bridges, baths, schools and fountains carry the name of one man: Mimar Sinan, the most famous architect of the Ottoman Empire.

We do not know his exact birthday. Most historians think he was born around 1490 in a village near Kayseri, in central Anatolia. As a young man he was taken into the Ottoman system that trained boys for the army and the palace. He learned carpentry first, and then he became a soldier in the Janissary army.

Being a soldier turned out to be a good school for a builder. The army needed bridges, roads and boats, and Sinan was very good at building them quickly. One famous story says that during a campaign in 1538, the army had to cross the Prut River. Other engineers could not do it, but Sinan built a bridge in about two weeks. The soldiers and the sultan were amazed.

Soon after that, Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent made him the chief architect of the empire. Sinan kept this job for about fifty years and worked for three sultans. He was not only a designer. He also managed hundreds of workers, planned water systems for the city and checked the quality of every stone.

Sinan himself described his life's work in three steps. He called the Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul his "apprentice work", the first building of a student. The Süleymaniye Mosque, finished in 1557, was his "journeyman work", the work of a skilled builder. And the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne was his "masterpiece". He finished it when he was over eighty years old.

The Selimiye is a wonderful building. Its great dome seems to float in the air, and its four tall, thin minarets rise like pencils into the sky. Inside, light comes in through many windows, so the huge space feels light and calm. Sinan was proud that its dome was as wide as, or even wider than, the dome of Hagia Sophia, which had been the model for builders for almost a thousand years.

Sinan also cared about sound and safety. In the Süleymaniye, people say he placed empty pots inside the dome to make voices clearer. He also designed his buildings to stand strong during earthquakes, and many of them have survived for more than four hundred years in a city that often shakes.

More than three hundred buildings are linked to his name, although not all of them were built by him personally. Many were built by his students, who later spread his style across the empire.

Sinan died in 1588, when he was nearly a hundred years old. He was buried in a small, simple tomb next to the Süleymaniye, the mosque he loved. He designed the tomb himself. After building so many great domes for sultans, he chose a very modest place for his own rest.

questions.q: How did Sinan first become famous as a builder?
options: He built a bridge very quickly for the army.
He designed a palace for his village.
He wrote a book about domes.
He repaired Hagia Sophia.
questions.explain: Metinde Sinan'ın 1538'deki bir seferde Prut Nehri üzerine yaklaşık iki haftada köprü kurduğu ve herkesi şaşırttığı anlatılıyor. Doğru cevap "He built a bridge very quickly for the army."

questions.q: Which building did Sinan call his "masterpiece"?
options: The Şehzade Mosque
The Süleymaniye Mosque
His own tomb
The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne
questions.explain: Sinan Şehzade'yi çıraklık, Süleymaniye'yi kalfalık, Edirne'deki Selimiye'yi ise ustalık eseri olarak görüyordu. Doğru cevap "The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne".

title: The Traveller Who Never Went Home
text:
In June 1325, a young man of twenty-one left his home in Tangier, a city in Morocco. His name was Ibn Battuta, and he planned to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He thought the trip would take about a year and a half. In fact, he did not come home for almost twenty-four years.

The beginning of the journey was not easy. He travelled alone at first, and he felt so lonely that he cried. Later he joined groups of merchants and pilgrims, because travelling in a large group was safer. On the way he became ill with a fever, but he tied himself to his saddle so that he would not fall off his animal.

After he reached Mecca, Ibn Battuta did not want to stop. He had a simple rule: he tried never to travel the same road twice. He went to Iraq and Persia, sailed down the coast of East Africa, and then came to Anatolia. He liked Anatolia very much. In many towns, groups of young men called the Ahi welcomed travellers, gave them food and a place to sleep, and asked for nothing in return. He wrote that he had never seen people so kind to strangers.

From there he crossed the Black Sea and went into Central Asia. Finally, he arrived in India. The sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, was a rich and strange ruler. He was very generous to his guests, but he could also be very cruel. He gave Ibn Battuta a job as a judge and a high salary. The traveller stayed for several years, but he was often afraid of the sultan's anger.

Later the sultan sent him on a mission to China with gifts. The trip was a disaster. His ship was destroyed in a storm, and he lost almost everything. Instead of going back to Delhi, he went to the Maldives, a group of small islands in the Indian Ocean. There he worked as a judge again and even married. In the end he did reach China, where he saw paper money and huge ships for the first time.

He returned to Morocco around 1349, only to learn that his mother had died of the plague some months earlier. Even then he did not stay still for long. He visited Spain, and then he crossed the Sahara Desert to the kingdom of Mali in West Africa.

When he finally settled down, the sultan of Morocco asked him to tell the story of his travels. A writer named Ibn Juzayy wrote down his words. The book, usually called the Rihla, which means "journey", describes about thirty years of travel. Some experts think he travelled more than 100,000 kilometres, a distance few people of his time could even imagine.

Not every detail in the book is true. Some parts were copied from other writers, and some places he may never have visited. But the Rihla is still one of the richest pictures we have of the world in the fourteenth century.

questions.q: What did Ibn Battuta write about the Ahi groups in Anatolia?
options: They sold him a new animal.
They did not let him enter their towns.
They were extremely kind and helpful to travellers.
They gave him a job as a judge.
questions.explain: Metne göre Ahi grupları yolculara yemek ve yatacak yer verip karşılık beklemiyordu; Ibn Battuta yabancılara bu kadar iyi davranan insanlar görmediğini yazdı. Doğru cevap "They were extremely kind and helpful to travellers."

questions.q: How was the Rihla written?
options: A writer wrote down the story that Ibn Battuta told.
Ibn Battuta wrote it every night during his trips.
His mother collected his letters.
The sultan of Delhi wrote it.
questions.explain: Fas sultanının isteğiyle Ibn Juzayy adlı bir yazar, Ibn Battuta'nın anlattıklarını yazıya geçirdi. Doğru cevap "A writer wrote down the story that Ibn Battuta told."

title: Barefoot in Rome
text:
On the evening of 10 September 1960, the marathon runners of the Rome Olympics were moving through the dark streets of the old city. Soldiers held torches along the road to light the way. Near the front of the race was a thin man from Ethiopia whom almost nobody knew. His name was Abebe Bikila, and he was running without shoes.

Abebe was born in 1932 in a small village in Ethiopia. As a boy he looked after animals and ran long distances across the hills, which are more than two thousand metres above the sea. Later he joined the Imperial Guard, the soldiers who protected the emperor, Haile Selassie. There a Swedish coach called Onni Niskanen noticed how strong he was and began to train him.

Abebe was not even supposed to run in Rome. He joined the team at the last minute because another runner was injured. When he arrived in Italy, the shoes that the team gave him did not fit well and hurt his feet. So he made a simple decision: he would run barefoot, as he did at home in training.

Before the race, his coach told him to watch one runner in particular, a Moroccan athlete wearing the number 26. But that runner was wearing a different number, so Abebe could not find him. He decided to run his own race. For most of the way he ran side by side with the Moroccan, Rhadi Ben Abdesselam, without knowing who he was.

With about a kilometre to go, Abebe ran faster and left the other man behind. He crossed the finish line near the Arch of Constantine, and he did not even look very tired. His time was about two hours and fifteen minutes, a new world best. He became the first Black African to win an Olympic gold medal. Later he said, in words that are still repeated today, that he wanted the world to know that his country had always won with courage.

Four years later, at the Tokyo Olympics, he ran again. This time he wore shoes. About six weeks before the race he had an operation on his stomach, and many people thought he could not run. But he won again, with another world best time, and became the first person to win the Olympic marathon twice. After the finish, he even did some exercises on the grass while the others were arriving.

His story has a sad ending. In 1969 he was badly hurt in a car accident and could not walk again. But he did not give up sport. He took part in archery competitions in a wheelchair, and he joined a dog-sled race in Norway. He died in 1973, when he was only forty-one years old.

In Ethiopia, Abebe Bikila is a national hero. His success in Rome showed young runners across Africa that they could compete with the best in the world, and many great Ethiopian runners followed him.

questions.q: Why did Abebe run without shoes in Rome?
options: His coach told him that shoes were slow.
He forgot his shoes in Ethiopia.
Running barefoot was a rule for Ethiopian runners.
The shoes he was given did not fit and hurt his feet.
questions.explain: Metne göre takımın verdiği ayakkabılar ayağına tam olmadı ve ayaklarını acıttı; bu yüzden evdeki gibi çıplak ayakla koştu. Doğru cevap "The shoes he was given did not fit and hurt his feet."

questions.q: What was special about his race in Tokyo?
options: He ran barefoot again.
He became the first person to win the Olympic marathon twice.
He lost to the Moroccan runner.
He ran in a wheelchair.
questions.explain: Tokyo'da ameliyattan kısa süre sonra yine kazandı ve olimpiyat maratonunu iki kez kazanan ilk kişi oldu. Doğru cevap "He became the first person to win the Olympic marathon twice."

title: A Girl Who Wanted to Fly
text:
Today millions of people fly every year from Sabiha Gökçen Airport in Istanbul. Many of them never ask who the airport is named after. The answer is a remarkable woman who became one of the first female military pilots in the world.

The future pilot was born in Bursa in 1913. She lost her parents when she was a child, and her life was not easy. In 1925, when Mustafa Kemal Atatürk visited Bursa, the young girl asked to speak to him. She told him that she wanted to go to school. The leader listened to her story and decided to adopt her. She moved to his home in Ankara and later studied at a girls' school in Istanbul.

In 1934 a new law asked every family in Turkey to choose a surname. He gave her the name Gökçen, which comes from the Turkish word for sky. At that time nobody knew how well the name would suit her.

The following year, in 1935, Atatürk took her to the opening of a new flying school called Türkkuşu. She watched the gliders and the parachute jumpers with great excitement. When Atatürk asked her whether she would like to learn to fly, she said yes at once. She became one of the school's first students. Soon she was sent to the Soviet Union for more training with gliders.

But Sabiha wanted more than gliders. She wanted to fly military aircraft. In 1936 she started training at the military flight school in Eskişehir. She was the only woman there, and she had to prove herself again and again. She trained with bombers and fighter planes, and in the following years she flew in real military operations. Because of this, she is often described as the world's first female combat pilot.

In 1938 she made a long flight around the Balkan countries. She visited cities such as Athens, Belgrade and Bucharest, and the newspapers there wrote about the young Turkish woman who flew her own plane. For many people in Europe, it was the first time they had heard of a female military pilot.

For Atatürk, her success had a clear meaning. It showed that women in the new republic could do any job, even the most difficult and dangerous ones. Young girls across the country read about her and started to dream of new careers.

Later Sabiha Gökçen became the chief trainer at Türkkuşu and taught many young pilots. She continued flying for many years and flew thousands of hours in total. She also wrote a book about her life with Atatürk. She died in Ankara in 2001, at the age of eighty-eight.

When Istanbul opened its second international airport in 2001, it was named after her. So every plane that takes off from there carries, in a small way, the memory of a girl who wanted to go to school and ended up in the sky.

questions.q: What did young Sabiha ask Atatürk for in Bursa?
options: A job at the airport
A chance to go to school
A ride in a plane
A new surname
questions.explain: Metne göre Sabiha, Atatürk'e okula gitmek istediğini söyledi. Doğru cevap "A chance to go to school".

questions.q: Why is the surname "Gökçen" a good name for her?
options: It was the name of her flying school.
It is the name of a city in the Balkans.
It comes from the Turkish word for sky.
It was her mother's family name.
questions.explain: "Gökçen" soyadı "gök" kelimesinden gelir; pilot olacak biri için çok uygun bir isimdi. Doğru cevap "It comes from the Turkish word for sky."

title: The Map on the Classroom Wall
text:
Think of the world map that hung on the wall of your classroom. Greenland probably looked enormous, almost as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is about fourteen times larger. This strange picture of the world comes from a map made more than four hundred and fifty years ago by a man called Gerardus Mercator.

He was born in 1512 in a small town in Flanders, in what is now Belgium. His family was poor, but an uncle who was a priest helped to pay for his education. As a young man he studied at the University of Leuven. He loved mathematics, the stars and geography, and he also had very skilful hands. He learned to engrave, which means cutting fine lines into metal plates for printing.

Soon he was making globes, scientific instruments and maps, and he became well known for his beautiful lettering. Even the emperor, Charles V, bought instruments from him. Life was not always safe, however. In 1544, at a time of religious conflict in Europe, he was arrested because the authorities thought he did not follow the official church. He spent about seven months in prison before he was finally set free. A few years later he moved to the town of Duisburg in Germany, where he lived for the rest of his life.

The great problem for mapmakers was simple to explain but very hard to solve. The Earth is round, but a map is flat. You cannot turn the skin of an orange into a flat sheet without stretching or tearing it. Every flat map changes the real shape of the world in some way.

Mercator decided to solve the problem for one special group of people: sailors. At sea, sailors used a compass and liked to follow a fixed direction, for example always south-west. In 1569 Mercator published a large world map with a clever design. On his map, a line with one fixed compass direction appeared as a straight line. A sailor could draw a line between two ports with a ruler and then follow that direction with the compass.

To make this possible, Mercator had to stretch the map more and more as he moved away from the equator. Near the poles, the land became much bigger than it really is. That is why Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia look so huge on many maps today, while countries near the equator look smaller than they are.

Mercator also gave us a word. He worked for years on a large book of maps, and he called it an "atlas", after a king from an old legend who studied the sky. The book was published in 1595, a year after his death. Since then, every book of maps has been called an atlas.

Today, many geographers prefer other maps for showing the true size of countries. But on the screens of our phones, online maps still use a version of his idea, because it keeps shapes correct when we zoom in on a street.

questions.q: Why was Mercator's map so useful for sailors?
options: It showed the true size of every country.
A fixed compass direction appeared as a straight line.
It was small enough to put in a pocket.
It showed all the dangerous rocks in the sea.
questions.explain: Mercator'un haritasında sabit pusula yönündeki bir rota düz bir çizgi olarak görünüyordu; denizci cetvelle çizip pusulayla izleyebiliyordu. Doğru cevap "A fixed compass direction appeared as a straight line."

questions.q: Why does Greenland look so big on many world maps?
options: The map is stretched more and more near the poles.
Greenland is really bigger than Africa.
Mercator made a mistake in his measurements.
Sailors wanted to see Greenland clearly.
questions.explain: Mercator ekvatordan uzaklaştıkça haritayı daha çok germek zorunda kaldı; bu yüzden kutuplara yakın yerler gerçekte olduğundan büyük görünür. Doğru cevap "The map is stretched more and more near the poles."

title: Frida and the Mirror
text:
In a quiet street in Mexico City there is a bright blue house. Today it is a museum, and thousands of visitors come every year to see where one of the world's most famous painters lived. Her name was Frida Kahlo, and her life was full of pain, colour and courage.

Frida was born in this blue house in 1907. Her father was a photographer, and she was close to him. When she was six years old, she became ill with polio. She had to stay in bed for months, and after that her right leg stayed thinner than the left one. Some children at school laughed at her. To make her stronger, her father encouraged her to do sports such as swimming and even boxing, which was very unusual for a girl at that time.

As a teenager, Frida was clever and full of life. She was one of very few girls at one of the best schools in the country, and she wanted to become a doctor. But in 1925, when she was eighteen, everything changed. The bus she was riding in crashed into a tram. A metal bar went through her body, and her back, her leg and her foot were broken in many places. For a long time, nobody was sure if she would live.

She spent months in bed, covered in plaster. She was bored and in pain. To help her, her mother put a mirror above her bed, and her father lent her his paints. Frida started to paint the person she saw every day in the mirror: herself. Later she explained that she painted herself because she was so often alone, and because she was the subject she knew best.

When she could walk again, she took her paintings to Diego Rivera, the most famous painter in Mexico. She asked him for an honest opinion. He liked her work very much. They fell in love and married in 1929. Their marriage was stormy, with many arguments, and they even divorced and married again. But they always stayed important to each other.

Frida's paintings are small, colourful and very personal. She often wore traditional Mexican dresses and flowers in her hair, and she painted herself with monkeys, parrots and plants. In some paintings she showed her pain openly, with broken columns or tears on her face. Her health was never good. During her life she had many operations, perhaps more than thirty.

In 1953, her first solo exhibition in Mexico opened. Her doctors told her not to go because she was too ill. So she arrived in an ambulance, and her bed was carried into the gallery. She lay there, greeted her friends and enjoyed the evening.

She died the next year, at the age of forty-seven. For a long time she was known mostly as Rivera's wife. Today, however, she is one of the best-known artists of the twentieth century, and her face, with its strong dark eyebrows, appears on posters and bags all over the world.

questions.q: Why did Frida begin to paint herself?
options: Diego Rivera asked her to paint him.
Her school gave her a painting class.
She was in bed and could see herself in a mirror every day.
A museum asked her for a self-portrait.
questions.explain: Kazadan sonra yatakta yatarken annesi yatağın üstüne ayna koydu; Frida her gün gördüğü kişiyi, yani kendini çizmeye başladı. Doğru cevap "She was in bed and could see herself in a mirror every day."

questions.q: How did Frida attend her exhibition in 1953?
options: She did not go because her doctors said no.
She walked in with Diego Rivera.
She watched it on television.
She arrived in an ambulance and lay in her bed in the gallery.
questions.explain: Doktorlar gitmemesini söyleyince ambulansla geldi ve yatağı galeriye taşındı. Doğru cevap "She arrived in an ambulance and lay in her bed in the gallery."

title: Twelve Seconds in the Air
text:
One day in 1878, a father came home with a small present for his two sons. It was a toy made of paper, wood and a rubber band. When the boys let it go, it flew up to the ceiling. The boys, Wilbur and Orville Wright, played with it until it broke, and then they built their own copies. Many years later, they said that this little toy was where their interest in flying began.

The brothers grew up in Dayton, Ohio, in the United States. Neither of them finished high school, but they were good with machines and they loved to read. In the 1890s, bicycles were very popular, so they opened a bicycle shop. They repaired bicycles, and later they designed and built their own. This work gave them money for their experiments and taught them a lot about light, strong machines.

At that time, many people were trying to build flying machines. Some were famous scientists with plenty of money. Most of their machines crashed. The Wright brothers believed that the biggest problem was not power, but control. A pilot had to be able to keep the machine balanced in the wind, just like a cyclist on a bicycle.

So they watched birds very carefully. They noticed that birds change the shape of their wings to turn and to stay balanced. The brothers found a way to twist the ends of a plane's wings with wires. They tested their ideas with kites and then with gliders. When their results did not match the numbers in other scientists' books, they built a small wind tunnel in their shop and tested about two hundred different wing shapes.

To test their gliders, they needed strong, steady wind and soft sand for landing. They found both at Kitty Hawk, on the coast of North Carolina. They travelled there every autumn for several years and lived in a simple wooden camp.

In 1903 they were ready to try a plane with an engine. They could not find a light enough engine, so their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, built one for them. They also designed their own propellers. On 14 December, the brothers threw a coin to decide who would fly first. Wilbur won, but the plane rose too steeply and came down after a few seconds.

Three days later, on 17 December 1903, it was Orville's turn. At about half past ten in the morning, the plane moved along its wooden track and rose into the cold wind. It stayed in the air for about twelve seconds and flew about thirty-seven metres, less than the length of a modern passenger plane. But it was the first time a powered machine with a pilot had flown under control. That day they made four flights. The longest, by Wilbur, lasted almost a minute.

Surprisingly, very few people believed them at first. Only a few newspapers reported the story. It was not until 1908, when Wilbur flew in front of large crowds in France, that the world finally understood what the two brothers from the bicycle shop had done.

questions.q: According to the brothers, what was the biggest problem in building a flying machine?
options: Finding enough money
Finding a strong engine
Finding soft sand
Controlling and balancing the machine
questions.explain: Metne göre Wright kardeşler asıl sorunun güç değil kontrol olduğuna inanıyordu: pilot makineyi rüzgârda dengede tutabilmeliydi. Doğru cevap "Controlling and balancing the machine".

questions.q: What happened on 17 December 1903?
options: Orville made the first controlled flight of a powered plane.
Wilbur flew in front of large crowds in France.
The brothers opened their bicycle shop.
The plane crashed after a coin was thrown.
questions.explain: 17 Aralık 1903'te Orville, motorlu ve pilotlu bir makineyle ilk kontrollü uçuşu yaptı. Doğru cevap "Orville made the first controlled flight of a powered plane."

title: The Pocket Hercules
text:
He was only about one metre and forty-seven centimetres tall, and he weighed around sixty kilos. But when Naim Süleymanoğlu stepped onto the stage, the whole hall became silent. Within a few seconds, he could lift a bar three times heavier than his own body. The world called him the "Pocket Hercules".

Naim was born in 1967 in a mountain village in southern Bulgaria, into a family of Bulgarian Turks. He was small but very strong, and a coach saw his talent when he was a child. He started training in a sports school, and he trained for many hours every day. As a teenager he was already breaking world records.

But in the 1980s, life became very difficult for the Turks of Bulgaria. The government forced them to change their names to Bulgarian ones. Naim was given a new name, and his records were written under it. He did not want to lose his identity, and he decided to leave the country.

His chance came in 1986, during a competition in Melbourne, Australia. One evening, while his team was having dinner, he quietly left the restaurant and asked for help. With the support of Turkish officials, he flew to London and then to Turkey. When he landed in Ankara, crowds were waiting for him, and many people cried with joy.

There was one more problem. According to the rules, an athlete who changed countries had to wait several years before competing in the Olympics for a new country. In the end, an agreement was made, and Turkey reportedly paid Bulgaria about a million dollars. So Naim was free to compete for Turkey at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.

In Seoul he was simply amazing. He broke several world records in one evening. In one lift he raised 190 kilos above his head, more than three times his body weight. Millions of people in Turkey watched him on television, and he came home as a national hero.

He did not stop there. He won gold medals again in Barcelona in 1992 and in Atlanta in 1996. With this, he became the first weightlifter in history to win three Olympic gold medals. The competition in Atlanta was especially exciting. He and a Greek lifter, who was also a friend of his, broke world records one after another. In the end, Naim won by just a few kilos, and the two men hugged each other on the stage.

After his sporting life, Naim tried politics for a short time, but he was never as comfortable there as he had been on the stage. His health became poor, and he died in Istanbul in 2017, when he was only fifty years old.

People in Turkey still remember the nights when the whole country stayed awake to watch him. For many, he was more than a sportsman. He was a symbol of courage, hard work and the joy of coming home.

questions.q: Why did Naim decide to leave Bulgaria?
options: He wanted to train in Australia.
He did not want to lose his name and identity.
His coach moved to Turkey.
He wanted to become a politician.
questions.explain: Bulgar hükümeti Türklerin isimlerini değiştirmeye zorladı; Naim kimliğini kaybetmek istemediği için ülkeden ayrılmaya karar verdi. Doğru cevap "He did not want to lose his name and identity."

questions.q: What did Naim achieve for the first time in history?
options: He won three Olympic gold medals in weightlifting.
He lifted four times his body weight.

He competed in five Olympics.
