title: The Race to the South Pole
text:
As a teenager in Norway, Roald Amundsen read about the explorers of the Arctic and made a secret decision: he would become a polar explorer too. According to a well-known story, he even slept with his bedroom window open in winter so his body would get used to the cold. His mother wanted him to be a doctor, and he started to study medicine. But after she died, he left university and went to sea.

The young Norwegian believed that an explorer should learn from people who already lived in the cold. Between 1903 and 1906, he and a small crew sailed a little fishing boat called the Gjøa through the icy waters north of Canada. They became the first people to sail all the way through the famous Northwest Passage. During two winters there, Amundsen lived near the Inuit. He learned how they dressed in animal fur, how they built shelters and, above all, how they travelled with dogs.

His next dream was the North Pole. But in 1909, while he was preparing, news came that two Americans each said they had reached it. So he quietly changed his plan. He sailed south in his ship, the Fram, and told almost nobody. When the ship reached the island of Madeira, he finally told his crew that they were going to Antarctica. He also sent a short message to a British explorer, Robert Falcon Scott, who was already on his way there. Now it was a race.

The two teams used very different methods. The British team took motor sledges, ponies and dogs, and his men often pulled the sledges themselves. The Norwegians trusted dogs and skis. His men were excellent skiers, and they wore fur clothes like the Inuit. During the winter, they prepared everything carefully and left stores of food along the route.

On 20 October 1911, Amundsen and four companions started for the Pole with four sledges and about fifty dogs. The journey was very hard. They climbed a huge glacier into the mountains and crossed fields of dangerous cracks in the ice. On 14 December 1911, they reached the South Pole. They put up a small tent with the Norwegian flag and left a letter for Scott inside. Then they turned back, and all five men returned safely.

The British team arrived at the Pole about five weeks later, on 17 January 1912. When they saw the Norwegian flag, they were deeply disappointed. On the long way back, the weather was terrible and they did not have enough food. The British leader and his four companions all died.

The Norwegian became famous, but he was always a little sad that people talked so much about Scott's tragedy. He continued exploring, and in 1926 he flew over the North Pole in an airship. In 1928 he flew north again to help in the search for a lost team of explorers. His plane disappeared over the Arctic sea, and he was never found.

questions.q: What did Amundsen learn from the Inuit?
options: How to build motor sledges
How to sail through the Northwest Passage
How to dress in fur and travel with dogs
How to fly an airship
questions.explain: Amundsen Inuitlerden hayvan kürkü giymeyi, barınak yapmayı ve özellikle köpeklerle yolculuk etmeyi öğrendi. Doğru cevap "How to dress in fur and travel with dogs".

questions.q: What did Scott's team find when they reached the South Pole?
options: A store of food from Amundsen
Nothing, because they were the first
A group of Inuit
A Norwegian tent and flag
questions.explain: Scott'un ekibi Kutba vardığında Norveç bayrağını ve çadırını gördü; Amundsen onlardan yaklaşık beş hafta önce gelmişti. Doğru cevap "A Norwegian tent and flag".

title: A City Under the Ground
text:
Most people come to Cappadocia to look up at the sky. They want to see the balloons, the strange rock towers and the sunset over the valleys. On my second day there, my friend Deniz had a different idea. "Today," she said, "we are going down."

We took a small bus to Derinkuyu, a quiet town about thirty kilometres from Göreme. From the main street, nothing looked special. There were a few shops, a tea garden and some old men playing backgammon. Then we walked through a simple door, paid for our tickets, and started to go down a narrow stone stairway.

The air changed almost at once. Outside it was a hot summer afternoon, but under the ground it was cool and a little damp. The walls were soft, light brown rock, and we could still see the marks of the tools that people used to dig them many centuries ago. Small lamps showed the way through long, low tunnels. Deniz is quite tall, and she had to bend her back most of the time.

Our guide, a friendly man called Mehmet, explained that Derinkuyu is one of the largest underground cities in the region. It has several levels, and the deepest parts are probably more than sixty metres below the ground. Nobody knows exactly when people started digging here. Some parts may be very old, and later generations made the city bigger and bigger. In dangerous times, the guide said, thousands of people may have lived here for weeks, together with their animals and their food.

We saw rooms for every need. There were kitchens with black smoke marks on the ceiling, stables for animals, places to store wine and oil, and even a small church. Long, deep holes went straight up to the surface. These were for fresh air, and some of them also reached water. Mehmet stopped next to a huge, round stone that looked like a giant wheel. "This was the door," he said. "People rolled it across the tunnel from the inside. An enemy could not open it from the other side."

The story of how the city was found again is also interesting. In the 1960s, a local man was repairing his house. When he knocked down a wall, he found a dark passage behind it. That passage led to this enormous hidden world. Today visitors can only see a part of it, because many tunnels are closed for safety.

After about an hour, we climbed back up into the bright light. My legs were tired, and my eyes needed a minute to get used to the sun. Deniz smiled and said, "Now you can look at the balloons again." But I could not stop thinking about the families who once lived in the dark, quietly waiting for danger to pass above their heads.

questions.q: Why did people probably live in the underground city?
options: To stay safe in dangerous times
To hide from the summer heat only
To work in large wine factories
To watch the balloons in the morning
questions.explain: Rehber, tehlikeli zamanlarda binlerce kişinin burada yaşamış olabileceğini söylüyor; doğru cevap "To stay safe in dangerous times".

questions.q: How was the city found again in the 1960s?
options: A guide followed a cat into a hole
Scientists used special machines
A man found a passage behind a wall in his house
Children fell into an air hole
questions.explain: Metne göre evini tamir eden bir adam duvarı yıkınca arkasında karanlık bir geçit buldu; doğru cevap "A man found a passage behind a wall in his house".

title: The Night Train to Bergen
text:
I have always loved trains, but I had never slept on one until last winter. I was visiting Norway for a week, and a friend told me about the railway between Oslo and Bergen. "Take the night train," she said. "You will wake up in another world."

The train left Oslo late in the evening. My ticket was for a small sleeping room with two narrow beds, a tiny sink and a window. I shared it with nobody, so I had space for my bag and a cup of hot chocolate from the café car. For the first hour, I watched the lights of small towns and quiet farms go past in the dark. Then the houses disappeared, and there was only snow.

The line between the two cities is often called one of the most beautiful train journeys in Europe. It opened in 1909, and building it was very hard work. The railway climbs over a wide, high plateau called Hardangervidda, where the weather can be extreme for much of the year. At its highest point, near a tiny place called Finse, the train is more than a thousand metres above the sea. In winter, special machines must keep the tracks free of snow.

I wanted to stay awake for that part, but the soft movement of the train was stronger than me. I fell asleep with my face near the window. Some time later, I woke up because the train had stopped. Outside, everything was white and blue under the moon. There were no trees, no roads and no people. Snow was falling slowly onto the platform of a station with only one small building. A worker in an orange jacket walked past, waved at the train, and disappeared into the night. It felt like a scene from a film.

When I woke up again, it was morning, and the view had changed completely. We were going down through deep valleys now. There were frozen waterfalls on the rocks, dark green forests and red wooden houses next to the water. In winter the days are very short in Norway, so the sky was still grey and pink.

We arrived in Bergen at around seven o'clock. The city is famous for its colourful old wooden buildings near the harbour and for its rain, and it was raining, of course. I did not mind at all. I walked to a small café, ordered coffee and a cinnamon bun, and wrote a long message to my friend.

"You were right," I wrote. "I went to sleep in one world and woke up in another." Since that trip, when people ask me for travel advice, I always say the same thing: if you can, take the slow train, and take it at night.

questions.q: What did the writer see when the train stopped in the night?
options: A busy city full of people
A small snowy station and a worker in an orange jacket
Red houses next to the sea
A café with hot chocolate
questions.explain: Tren gece durduğunda yazar tek binalı küçük, karlı bir istasyon ve turuncu ceketli bir işçi görüyor; doğru cevap "A small snowy station and a worker in an orange jacket".

questions.q: What advice does the writer give at the end?
options: Always fly between big cities
Visit Norway only in summer
Never travel alone in winter
Take the slow train at night if possible
questions.explain: Yazar sonunda mümkünse yavaş treni ve geceleyin seçmeyi öneriyor; doğru cevap "Take the slow train at night if possible".

title: Evening in a Marrakesh Square
text:
Our plane landed in Marrakesh in the afternoon, and by six o'clock my sister Selin and I were standing at the edge of Jemaa el-Fnaa, the famous main square of the old city. We had read about it before the trip, but nothing had prepared us for the noise, the smells and the energy of the place.

During the day, the square is quite open and dusty. There are orange juice sellers with their carts, women who draw henna patterns on visitors' hands, and men selling small cups of fresh mint tea. But as the sun goes down, the square slowly changes. Workers bring tables, benches and metal frames, and in less than an hour, dozens of food stalls appear, each with a number and a cloud of white smoke above it.

We walked slowly between the stalls. One man was cooking small pieces of lamb on long sticks. Another was selling snails in a spicy soup, served in little bowls. Selin wanted to try them, but I was not brave enough. In the end, we sat on a bench at stall number thirty-one and ordered grilled vegetables, bread, and a tagine, a dish cooked slowly in a clay pot with a tall, pointed top. It was delicious.

Around the food stalls, there were circles of people. In the middle of one circle, musicians were playing drums and long-necked instruments. In another, an old man was telling a story in Arabic. We did not understand a single word, but we watched his hands and his face, and we laughed when everyone else laughed. Storytellers have entertained people in this square for centuries. UNESCO lists the square's oral traditions as part of the world's cultural heritage, and many people believe it is important to protect them.

Behind the square, narrow streets lead into the souks, the old markets of the city. In the evening, they are full of light from metal lamps with tiny holes in them. We saw leather bags, colourful carpets, silver jewellery and piles of spices in red, yellow and orange. Every seller invited us inside for a "good price". Selin bargained for a small lamp, and after ten minutes of friendly discussion, they agreed on half of the first price. The seller laughed and said, "You are a hard customer!"

Later, we climbed to the terrace of a café above the square. From there, the whole place looked like a giant stage. The smoke from the stalls rose into the dark sky, and in the distance we could see the tall tower of the Koutoubia Mosque, lit up in gold. The call to prayer mixed with the sound of the drums.

"Do you want to come back tomorrow?" Selin asked. I did not even need to answer.

questions.q: What happens in the square when the sun goes down?
options: It becomes empty and quiet
Workers close it to visitors
Dozens of food stalls appear
Only juice sellers stay
questions.explain: Güneş batarken işçiler masa ve tezgâh kuruyor ve onlarca yemek tezgâhı ortaya çıkıyor; doğru cevap "Dozens of food stalls appear".

questions.q: How did Selin get the lamp?
options: She bargained and paid about half the first price
She got it as a free gift
She paid the first price without talking
She bought it at the airport
questions.explain: Selin pazarlık etti ve satıcıyla ilk fiyatın yarısında anlaştı; doğru cevap "She bargained and paid about half the first price".

title: Windmills and Grapes on Bozcaada
text:
Every September, my grandmother tells the same story. When she was young, she spent one summer on Bozcaada, a small island in the north Aegean, and she says it was the best summer of her life. Last year, I finally decided to see the island for myself, and I took her with me.

We drove from İzmir to the coast near Çanakkale and left the car at the small port of Geyikli. The ferry was full of families, cyclists and a few trucks carrying fruit and building materials. The trip took only about half an hour. My grandmother stood at the front of the ship the whole time, holding her hat and looking at the island as it slowly grew bigger.

Bozcaada is not large. You can drive around it in less than an hour, and many visitors explore it by bicycle. The first thing you see from the ferry is the castle, a strong stone building next to the harbour. People have built and rebuilt it many times through history, because the island was always important for ships going to and from the Dardanelles.

Behind the harbour, there is a small town with narrow streets, white and blue houses, and wooden balconies covered with flowers. In the mornings, the smell of fresh bread and coffee fills the air. My grandmother walked slowly through the streets and stopped often. "This bakery was here," she said, pointing at a shop. "But it was much smaller." She was very happy when an old woman in the shop told her that it was the same family.

The island is famous for its vineyards. Grapes have grown here for a very long time, and the warm sun and strong winds suit them well. In September, the harvest begins, and you can see people working between the green rows with baskets. We visited a small family winery, where a young woman explained how they make wine from local grapes. My grandmother was more interested in another local product: tomato jam. It sounds strange, but it is sweet and surprisingly good with cheese.

On the west side of the island, the wind is very strong, and there is a long line of modern wind turbines on the hill. Near them, you can still see a few old stone windmills. In the past, people used them to grind wheat into flour. Today they are mostly a place for photographs, especially at sunset.

On our last evening, we sat on a beach and watched the sun go down behind the sea. The sky turned orange, then pink, then dark blue. My grandmother was quiet for a long time. Then she held my hand and said, "It has changed, but it is still my island." I understood then why she had told the story so many times.

questions.q: Why was the castle important in the past?
options: Kings lived there in summer
It protected the vineyards from the wind
Ships going to and from the Dardanelles passed the island
It was used to make flour
questions.explain: Metne göre ada, Çanakkale Boğazı’na gidip gelen gemiler için önemliydi, bu yüzden kale defalarca yapıldı; doğru cevap "Ships going to and from the Dardanelles passed the island".

questions.q: What made the grandmother very happy in the town?
options: She learned that the bakery belonged to the same family
She found her old house for sale
She won a bicycle race
She met an old school friend on the ferry
questions.explain: Fırındaki yaşlı kadın, dükkânın hâlâ aynı aileye ait olduğunu söyleyince büyükanne çok seviniyor; doğru cevap "She learned that the bakery belonged to the same family".

title: A Thousand Red Gates in Kyoto
text:
I set my alarm for half past five. It was my third day in Kyoto, and I had already learned one important lesson about the city: if you want to see its most famous places in peace, you must get there before everyone else.

So, while the streets were still dark and empty, I took the first train to Fushimi Inari, a shrine in the south of the city. The station is right in front of the entrance, and when I arrived, there were only two other people there, an old man with a dog and a woman jogging in sports clothes.

Fushimi Inari is famous for its torii, the traditional Japanese gates that mark the entrance to a holy place. Here there are not one or two of them, but thousands. They are painted a bright orange-red, and they stand so close together that they form long tunnels. These tunnels climb up the side of Mount Inari, a forested hill behind the main buildings.

As I started to walk, the sun came up, and light came through the small spaces between the gates. The colour on the ground and on my hands changed from grey to orange. It was completely quiet except for the birds and my own footsteps. I understood why so many people call this one of the most beautiful walks in Japan.

Each gate has black writing on one side. At first I thought it was a poem or a prayer, but a sign explained something different. The gates are gifts. Companies and individuals pay for them and write their names and the date on them. Inari is traditionally the god of rice, and over time many people also began to pray to Inari for success in business. A small gate may cost a few hundred thousand yen, and a large one costs much more.

Along the path, I also saw many stone statues of foxes. Some of them had red cloths around their necks, and some held a key or a ball in their mouths. In Japanese tradition, foxes are believed to be the messengers of Inari. They looked serious and a little mysterious in the morning light.

The full walk to the top of the mountain and back can take two or three hours. It is longer and steeper than many visitors expect. Halfway up, I found a small tea house with a view over the whole city. I sat down, ordered green tea and watched Kyoto wake up below me.

When I came back down at around nine o'clock, the paths were already full of tour groups, families and people taking selfies. The peaceful tunnels had become noisy and crowded. I was glad that I had come early. Sometimes the best part of travelling is not the place itself, but the moment you choose to see it.

questions.q: What is written on each gate?
options: A poem about the mountain
The names of the people or companies who gave it, and a date
Rules for visitors
The price of green tea
questions.explain: Tabelaya göre kapılar hediyedir ve üzerlerine bağışlayan kişi veya şirketin adı ile tarih yazılır; doğru cevap "The names of the people or companies who gave it, and a date".

questions.q: What lesson does the writer learn in Kyoto?
options: Tour groups are the best way to travel
Foxes are dangerous in the forest
The walk to the top takes only twenty minutes
Famous places are best visited early, before the crowds
questions.explain: Yazar ünlü yerleri sakin görmek için herkesten önce gitmek gerektiğini öğreniyor; doğru cevap "Famous places are best visited early, before the crowds".

title: A Weekend in Safranbolu
text:
When Kerem and I planned a short weekend trip from Ankara, we wanted something quiet, close and different from the big city. A colleague suggested Safranbolu. "It is like walking into the past," she said. She was right.

The bus journey took about three hours. Safranbolu is in the province of Karabük, in the north of Türkiye, and the newer part of the town looks like any other modern town. But the old town, which people call Çarşı, sits in a deep valley, and when you walk down into it, you suddenly find yourself in an Ottoman town of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The most famous thing about Safranbolu is its old houses. There are hundreds of them, and many are still in good condition. They usually have two or three floors, white walls, dark wooden beams and red tiled roofs. The upper floors are often wider than the ground floor, so they hang a little over the street. Because the houses are built on a hill, almost every one of them has a view and gets plenty of sunlight. In 1994, UNESCO added the town to its World Heritage List, and since then many houses have been carefully restored.

We stayed in one of these houses, which is now a small hotel. Our room had a low wooden ceiling with beautiful patterns, a large window with a view of the valley, and cupboards built into the walls. The owner showed us something surprising: a small bathroom hidden inside one of the cupboards. "In the past," he said, "people saved space in every way they could."

In the centre of the old town, there is a large stone building called Cinci Han. It was built in the seventeenth century as a caravanserai, a kind of hotel for traders who travelled with their camels and goods. Today it is a hotel again, and you can climb onto its roof for a wonderful view of the town.

The name of the town probably comes from saffron, a very expensive spice that is made from the small red parts of a purple flower. Saffron has been grown in the area for a long time, although today the amount is small. You can find it in many shops, together with the town's other famous product, lokum. We visited an old lokum shop where the seller let us taste six or seven kinds. My favourite had walnuts inside.

On Sunday morning, we walked to a quiet hill above the town and watched the mist slowly leave the valley. The roofs appeared one by one, red and shining after the night's rain. Kerem took dozens of photographs, but later he said that none of them showed how it really felt. I think he was right. Some places you simply have to see with your own eyes.

questions.q: Why does almost every house in Safranbolu get a view and sunlight?
options: Because the houses are built on a hill
Because they have glass roofs
Because the streets are very wide
Because there are no trees in the town
questions.explain: Evler bir yamaca kurulduğu için neredeyse hepsinin manzarası ve bol güneşi var; doğru cevap "Because the houses are built on a hill".

questions.q: What was Cinci Han in the past?
options: A spice factory
A school for children
A caravanserai where traders stayed
A Turkish bath
questions.explain: Cinci Han on yedinci yüzyılda tüccarlar için bir kervansaray olarak yapıldı; doğru cevap "A caravanserai where traders stayed".

title: Golden Stones of Mardin
text:
I arrived in Mardin late at night, so my first real view of the city came the next morning. I opened the window of my small hotel room, and below me there was a sea of flat roofs, stone walls and narrow stairways. Beyond them, the land fell away into a huge, flat plain that disappeared into a light brown mist. Someone in the hotel told me that on clear days you can see all the way to Syria.

The old city of Mardin is built on the side of a steep hill, and most of its buildings are made from the same local stone. It is a soft, yellowish stone, and its colour changes during the day. In the early morning it looks almost white, at noon it is pale gold, and at sunset it turns warm orange. Because the stone is soft, local craftsmen have been able to cut detailed patterns into doors, windows and walls for centuries.

The main street runs along the hill from one end of the old city to the other. Everything else goes up or down. There are hundreds of steps, small tunnels under houses, and tiny streets so narrow that donkeys are still sometimes used to carry rubbish and heavy things. I saw one with two big bags on its back, slowly climbing a stairway while its owner walked behind it, talking on his phone.

Mardin has a long and mixed history. Over the centuries, Muslims, Christians and other communities have lived here, and you can see this in the buildings. I visited the Zinciriye Medrese, an old school from the fourteenth century with a beautiful courtyard and a view over the plain. A few minutes away, there was an old church with a small, quiet garden. Outside the city, there is also a famous monastery called Deyrulzafaran, which some people believe is more than fifteen hundred years old.

In the afternoon, I walked through the bazaar. There were shops selling soap made with local herbs, bags of almonds and dried fruits, and a kind of coffee called menengiç, made from the seeds of a wild tree. A friendly shop owner insisted that I try a cup. It was creamy and a little like pistachio. I also watched an old man making fine silver jewellery with very thin wire, a traditional craft of the region called telkari.

That evening, I sat on the roof terrace of a café and waited for the sunset. As the light changed, the whole city seemed to glow. Families were drinking tea, children were running between the tables, and from somewhere below, I could hear a man singing. I had planned to stay in Mardin for two days, but the next morning I went to the hotel desk and asked for one more night.

questions.q: Why have craftsmen been able to cut detailed patterns into the buildings?
options: Because the local stone is soft
Because they used modern machines
Because the buildings are made of wood
Because the weather is always cool
questions.explain: Metne göre yerel taş yumuşak olduğu için ustalar yüzyıllardır kapı ve pencerelere ayrıntılı desenler oyabiliyor; doğru cevap "Because the local stone is soft".

questions.q: What did the writer decide at the end?
options: To leave the city early
To buy a silver ring
To visit Syria
To stay one more night
questions.explain: Yazar iki gün kalmayı planlamıştı ama ertesi sabah bir gece daha istedi; doğru cevap "To stay one more night".

title: The Little Yellow Tram of Lisbon
text:
On my first morning in Lisbon, I made a mistake that many visitors make. I tried to walk everywhere. The Portuguese capital is often called the city of seven hills, and after two hours of climbing up and down steep streets, my legs told me that this name was not a joke. So, in the afternoon, I decided to do what my guidebook recommended: take tram 28.

Lisbon has modern trams, but the ones on line 28 are old-fashioned and small. They are bright yellow, made partly of wood, and they look like toys. Many of them were built in the 1930s and have been repaired and updated since then. They are still used because they can climb steep hills and go around very sharp corners, where modern trams are too long to fit.

I got on at Martim Moniz, a square near the start of the line. The tram was already quite full, but I found a seat next to a window. The driver rang a bell, and we began to move with a lot of noise. Almost immediately, we were climbing a street so narrow that I could have touched the walls of the houses. People living there stood on their tiny balconies with washing hanging next to them, and some of them waved.

The tram took us through Graça and then into Alfama, the oldest part of the city. Alfama is a maze of small streets, stairways and little squares, and it survived the great earthquake of 1755 better than many other areas. From the window, I saw old churches, walls covered with blue and white tiles called azulejos, and short views of the river Tagus far below, shining in the sun.

At one corner, a car was parked in the wrong place, and the tram could not pass. The driver stopped, got out, and started talking to people in a café. After a few minutes, the owner of the car ran out with a coffee cup still in her hand and moved it. Nobody seemed angry. The passengers just smiled, as if this happened every day. Maybe it does.

The tram continued down to the Baixa, the flat centre of the city, with its wide streets and elegant squares, and then up again towards the area of Estrela. I got off near a small bakery and ordered a pastel de nata, a famous little cake with a warm, sweet cream filling. It was the perfect end to the ride.

A local woman I met later gave me two pieces of advice. First, ride the tram early in the morning or late in the evening, because in the middle of the day it is very crowded with tourists. Second, keep your bag in front of you, because crowded trams are popular with pickpockets. I followed both pieces of advice on my next ride, and it was even better.

questions.q: Why are the old trams still used on line 28?
options: They are cheaper than buses
They can climb steep hills and go around sharp corners
Tourists do not like modern trams
They are faster than modern trams
questions.explain: Eski tramvaylar dik yokuşlara çıkabildiği ve keskin virajlardan dönebildiği için hâlâ kullanılıyor; doğru cevap "They can climb steep hills and go around sharp corners".

questions.q: What happened when a car was parked in the wrong place?
options: The passengers got off and walked
The police took the car away
The tram driver hit the car
The owner came out of a café and moved it
questions.explain: Sürücü kafedekilerle konuştu ve arabanın sahibi elinde kahve fincanıyla çıkıp arabayı çekti; doğru cevap "The owner came out of a café and moved it".

title: Waiting for the Northern Lights
text:
For years, my brother Can had a photo of the northern lights as the background on his phone. Green waves of light over a snowy mountain. "One day I will see them with my own eyes," he always said. Last February, we finally flew to Iceland together to try.

The first thing we learned is that you cannot simply go outside and see the lights. Three things are necessary. First, it must be dark, so the best season is roughly from September to April, when the nights are long. Second, the sky must be clear, because the lights appear high above the clouds. Third, the sun must be active. The northern lights happen when tiny pieces from the sun travel through space and hit the gases in the air above the Earth. When this happens, the gases give off light, usually green, but sometimes pink or purple too.

In Iceland, people check a special forecast for the northern lights, just like a weather forecast. It shows the level of activity and a map of the clouds. On our first two nights, the map was almost completely grey. It was cloudy and windy, and we stayed in our guesthouse, playing cards and drinking hot tea. Can checked the forecast every half an hour. He was beginning to lose hope.

On the third day, we drove along the south coast. We saw huge waterfalls, black sand beaches and small horses with long hair standing in the wind. In the afternoon, the clouds started to move away, and the forecast changed. "Tonight," said the owner of our guesthouse, "you have a good chance. But go away from the lights of the town."

So, at around ten o'clock, we drove a few kilometres out of town and stopped next to a quiet field. We turned off the car lights and waited. It was very cold, perhaps ten degrees below zero, and I had two pairs of gloves on. The stars were incredibly bright. For almost an hour, nothing happened. Then Can pointed at the sky and said, very quietly, "Look."

At first it was just a pale band, like a thin grey cloud. I was not sure it was anything special. But slowly it became greener and brighter. Then it began to move, like a curtain in the wind. Waves of light danced from one side of the sky to the other, sometimes slowly, sometimes very fast. At one moment, a line of pink appeared at the bottom of the green. Neither of us said anything. We just stood there with our heads back and our mouths open.

The show lasted about twenty minutes, and then the light became weak again. Our hands and feet were frozen, but we were laughing like children. Back in the car, Can looked at his phone and changed his background. The new photo was not as sharp as the old one, but this time, he had taken it himself.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT necessary to see the northern lights, according to the text?
options: A dark night
A clear sky
Warm weather
Activity from the sun
questions.explain: Metinde gerekli üç şey karanlık, açık gökyüzü ve güneşin etkin olması olarak sayılıyor; sıcak hava gerekli değil, doğru cevap "Warm weather".

questions.q: Why did Can change the background on his phone?
options: Because the old photo was broken
Because his brother asked him to
Because he wanted a picture of a waterfall
Because now he had his own photo of the lights
questions.explain: Can artık ışıkların fotoğrafını kendisi çekmişti, bu yüzden arka planını değiştirdi; doğru cevap "Because now he had his own photo of the lights".

title: Taking the Bus in Venice
text:
When people imagine Venice, they usually think of gondolas, the long black boats with a man in a striped shirt standing at the back. Gondolas are beautiful, but they are also expensive, and most people who live in Venice rarely use them. If you want to travel like a local, you take the bus. In Venice, of course, the bus is a boat.

The water buses are called vaporetti. They are wide, slow boats with a covered area in the middle and open space at the front and back. There are many lines, and they stop at floating platforms all around the city and the nearby islands. My friend Aylin and I bought tickets for several days, which was much cheaper than paying for each trip.

On our first morning, we took line 1. This is the slowest line, because it stops at almost every station along the Grand Canal, the long, S-shaped waterway that runs through the middle of the city. But for a first-time visitor, slow is perfect. We found two places at the front of the boat and watched Venice pass by.

On both sides of the canal there were old palaces, painted pink, cream and red, with tall windows and wooden poles in the water in front of them. Some of the buildings looked tired, with paint coming off the walls, but this only made them more charming. We saw a delivery boat full of boxes of vegetables, a boat carrying furniture, and even a police boat with its blue lights on. In Venice there are no cars in the historic centre, so everything, from food to rubbish, travels on the water.

The city is built on more than a hundred small islands in a lagoon, connected by hundreds of bridges. One of the most famous is the Rialto Bridge, a white stone bridge with shops on it. When our boat passed under it, dozens of tourists on the bridge were taking photographs of us, and we were taking photographs of them.

An old man sitting next to us started a conversation. He had lived in Venice all his life. He told us that the number of people living in the old city has fallen a lot in recent decades, because houses are expensive and many apartments are rented to tourists. He also talked about the acqua alta, the high water that sometimes floods the streets, especially in autumn and winter. "We put on our boots and continue our day," he said with a shrug.

We got off at San Marco and walked into the huge square, full of pigeons and music from the cafés. In the evening, we took the vaporetto again, this time with the sun going down and the water turning gold. Aylin said it was the most beautiful bus ride of her life. I could not disagree.

questions.q: Why did the writer and Aylin take line 1?
options: It was the fastest line to the airport
It was slow and stopped at many places along the Grand Canal
It was the only line with a gondola
It was free for tourists
questions.explain: Hat 1, Büyük Kanal boyunca neredeyse her istasyonda durduğu için yavaş ve ilk kez gelenler için ideal; doğru cevap "It was slow and stopped at many places along the Grand Canal".

questions.q: According to the old man, why are fewer people living in the old city?
options: Because the water is too cold
Because there are no schools
Because houses are expensive and many are rented to tourists
Because the bridges are closed
questions.explain: Yaşlı adama göre evler pahalı ve birçok daire turistlere kiralanıyor; doğru cevap "Because houses are expensive and many are rented to tourists".

title: A Walk, a Dog and a Sticky Idea
titleTr: Bir yürüyüş, bir köpek ve yapışkan bir fikir
text:
In the early 1940s, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral went for a walk in the mountains with his dog. It was a normal day out, and nothing special seemed to happen. But when they came home, he noticed something annoying. Small, round seed heads from a wild plant were stuck all over his trousers and all over his dog's fur.

Most people would just pull them off and throw them away. De Mestral did that too, but he was also curious. Why did these little balls hold on so strongly? He took one and looked at it under a microscope. What he saw surprised him. The seed head was covered with hundreds of tiny hooks. These hooks caught on anything with small loops, like the threads of cloth or the hair of an animal.

Nature, he thought, had already invented a new way to join two things together. If he could copy it, people might close their clothes and bags without buttons or zips. It sounded simple, but it was not. For years, nobody could help him make the idea work. Many people laughed at it. In the end, he worked with weavers in Lyon, in France, and tried many materials. Cotton was too soft, and the hooks soon wore out. Finally, he discovered that nylon was strong enough. When nylon threads were cut in a certain way, they made very good hooks.

He made two strips of material. One strip had the hooks, and the other had soft loops. When you pressed them together, they held. When you pulled them apart, they made a loud tearing sound that many of us know today. De Mestral needed a name for his invention, so he joined two French words: velours, which means velvet, and crochet, which means hook. The result was "Velcro."

He received a patent for the idea in the mid-1950s, but at first, sales were slow. Some people thought the material looked cheap and ugly. Things changed in the 1960s, when the American space programme began to use it. Astronauts needed to keep pens, food packets and tools in place where there was no gravity. If Velcro was good enough for space, many people thought, it was good enough for Earth.

Today, you can find it on children's shoes, jackets, bags, hospital equipment and even some car seats. Small children who cannot tie their shoes yet can put them on by themselves. The story is also a good example of what scientists now call biomimicry: looking carefully at nature and borrowing its clever solutions.

So the next time a plant sticks to your clothes after a walk, do not just feel annoyed. Look closely. Perhaps there is another great idea hiding there, waiting for a curious mind.

questions.q: What gave George de Mestral the idea for his invention?
options: A broken zip on his jacket
Seed heads that stuck to his clothes and his dog
A book about space travel
A visit to a weaver in Lyon
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Seed heads that stuck to his clothes and his dog": yürüyüşten sonra pantolonuna ve köpeğinin tüylerine yapışan tohum kapsüllerini mikroskopla incelemiş.

questions.q: Why did more people start to accept Velcro in the 1960s?
options: It became much cheaper
Children asked for it
The space programme used it
Its tearing sound became quieter
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The space programme used it": Amerikan uzay programı kullanmaya başlayınca insanlar "uzay için yeterince iyiyse Dünya için de iyidir" diye düşünmüş.

title: The Chocolate Bar That Melted
text:
In 1945, an American engineer called Percy Spencer was working for a company that made equipment for radar. Radar was very important during the Second World War. It helped people find planes and ships far away by sending out invisible waves. One of the key parts of a radar system was a tube called a magnetron, which produced these waves.

According to the famous story, one day Spencer was standing next to a working magnetron. He had a chocolate bar in his pocket. When he reached for it later, he found that it had melted into a soft, sticky mess. The room was not hot, and he had not felt any heat on his body. So what had happened?

Many people might have just bought a new chocolate bar. Spencer, however, wanted to understand. He had very little formal education, because he had left school young to work, but he was a brilliant and curious engineer. He decided to test the waves with other foods. He put some corn near the magnetron, and soon it began to jump and pop. He had made popcorn. In another test, the story says, he tried an egg. It got hot very quickly and broke open, possibly near the face of a colleague who was watching too closely.

Spencer realised that the waves could heat food from the inside, and much faster than a normal oven. His company quickly asked for a patent, and in 1947 it sold the first microwave oven. It looked nothing like the small box in your kitchen today. It was almost as tall as a man and weighed hundreds of kilograms. It was also very expensive, so only restaurants, ships and trains bought it at first.

How does a microwave oven work? Most food contains water. The waves make the tiny parts of the water move back and forth billions of times every second. This fast movement creates heat, and the heat cooks the food. That is why dry plates often stay cool, while the soup on them gets hot. It is also why some parts of your meal can be very hot while other parts are still cold, so it is a good idea to stir food in the middle of heating.

Over the next decades, engineers made the ovens smaller, safer and cheaper. By the 1980s, millions of families had one at home. People started to use them for quick lunches, warm milk and, of course, popcorn on film nights.

Some historians say the chocolate story may be a little simpler than what really happened. Still, it shows something true about science. Discoveries often begin with a small surprise, and with a person who stops and asks, "Why?"

questions.q: What did Spencer do after he noticed the melted chocolate?
options: He tested the waves with other kinds of food
He stopped working with radar
He complained to his company
He bought a cooler suit
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "He tested the waves with other kinds of food": çikolatanın neden eridiğini anlamak için mısır ve yumurta gibi başka yiyeceklerle denemeler yapmış.

questions.q: According to the text, why can a plate stay cool while the soup gets hot?
options: Plates are made of metal
The oven only heats the top of the food
Soup is always cooked before it goes in
The waves mainly move water, and dry plates have little water
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The waves mainly move water, and dry plates have little water": dalgalar yiyecekteki suyu hareket ettirip ısı üretir; kuru tabakta su az olduğu için tabak ısınmaz.

title: The Octopus Who Left at Night
text:
One morning in 2016, workers at the National Aquarium of New Zealand arrived to find an empty tank. Inky, a male octopus, was gone. The night before, someone had left a small gap at the top of his tank. Wet marks on the floor seemed to show his path. Experts believe that he climbed out, moved across the floor and squeezed into a narrow pipe that led to the sea. He was never seen again. The story travelled around the world, and many people cheered for him.

Stories like this are not rare. Octopuses are famous for escaping, and they are very good at it. They have no bones, so they can push their soft bodies through any hole that is larger than their beak, which is the only hard part of their body. A big octopus can pass through a gap about the size of a coin.

But octopuses are not just flexible. They also seem to be surprisingly clever. In laboratories, they can learn to open jars with a screw top to reach a crab inside. Some have learned to recognise individual people. In one well-known report, an octopus did not like a particular worker and regularly shot water at her, but not at others. In the wild, some octopuses in Indonesia have been filmed carrying empty coconut shells across the sea floor. Later, they hide inside them, almost like a portable house.

Their bodies are strange in many ways. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. It can change the colour and even the texture of its skin in less than a second, so it can look like a rock, a plant or sand. Even more surprising, a large part of its nervous system is not in its head. About two thirds of its nerve cells are in its eight arms. Each arm can touch, taste and react on its own, while the brain makes the bigger decisions. Scientists are still trying to understand how the arms and the brain work together.

This is interesting because octopuses are very distant relatives of humans. Their family tree split from ours hundreds of millions of years ago, and they are more closely related to snails than to dogs or birds. So their intelligence probably developed in a completely separate way. Studying them may help us understand what intelligence really is, and how many different forms it can take.

There is one sad fact. Most octopuses live only one or two years. Some researchers think this short life is part of why they must learn so quickly. They do not have parents to teach them, so they have to solve problems by themselves. Somewhere in the ocean, Inky may still be solving them.

questions.q: How did Inky probably escape from the aquarium?
options: A worker carried him to the sea
He broke the glass of his tank
He went through a pipe that led to the sea
He hid inside a coconut shell
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "He went through a pipe that led to the sea": uzmanlara göre tanktan tırmanıp yerde ilerlemiş ve denize giden dar bir boruya girmiş.

questions.q: What is special about an octopus's nervous system?
options: Most of its nerve cells are in its arms
It has no brain at all
It is exactly like a human brain
It works only at night
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Most of its nerve cells are in its arms": sinir hücrelerinin yaklaşık üçte ikisi sekiz kolunda bulunur.

title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
text:
Almost every child asks it at some point: "Why is the sky blue?" Many parents give a quick answer, such as "because it reflects the sea." It is a nice idea, but it is not correct. The sky is blue even above deserts, far from any water. The real answer is more interesting, and it took scientists a long time to find it.

The story begins with sunlight. To our eyes, sunlight looks white or slightly yellow. But in the 1600s, Isaac Newton showed that white light is really a mix of all the colours of the rainbow. When light passes through a piece of glass with the right shape, it separates into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Each colour travels as a wave, and each one has a different wavelength. Red light has long waves, while blue and violet light have short waves.

Now think about the air. It looks empty, but it is full of tiny particles, mostly very small molecules of gas. When sunlight enters the air, it hits these molecules. The molecules send some of the light off in all directions. Scientists call this scattering. In the nineteenth century, the British scientists John Tyndall and Lord Rayleigh studied this process. Rayleigh showed that short waves are scattered much more strongly than long waves. So blue light bounces around the sky far more than red light does. Wherever you look, blue light is coming towards your eyes from all over the sky.

But wait. Violet light has even shorter waves. Why isn't the sky violet? There are a few reasons. The sun sends out less violet light than blue light, some violet light is absorbed high in the air, and our eyes are simply more sensitive to blue. Together, these facts make the sky look blue to us.

The same idea explains sunsets. In the evening, the sun is low, so its light has to travel through much more air before it reaches us. On this long journey, most of the blue light is scattered away. What is left is the orange and red light, which paints the clouds in warm colours.

Interestingly, the sky is not blue on every planet. On Mars, the air is very thin and full of fine red dust. Photos from robots on Mars show a pale, brownish sky during the day. At sunset, however, the sky around the sun can look slightly blue, which is the opposite of what we see on Earth.

So the next time a child asks you about the blue sky, you have a better answer. You can say that the air is playing with the sunlight, and that blue is the colour it likes to throw around the most.

questions.q: Why does the sky look blue during the day?
options: The sky reflects the colour of the sea
The sun sends out only blue light
Clouds are full of blue dust
Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Air molecules scatter blue light more than red light": havadaki moleküller kısa dalgalı mavi ışığı uzun dalgalı kırmızı ışıktan çok daha fazla saçar.

questions.q: Why are sunsets often orange and red?
options: The sun becomes cooler in the evening
The light travels through more air, and most of the blue is scattered away
Dust from Mars reaches the Earth
Our eyes get tired at the end of the day
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The light travels through more air, and most of the blue is scattered away": akşam güneş alçakta olduğu için ışık daha uzun yol alır ve mavi ışık saçılıp kaybolur.

title: The Man Who Hiccupped for Sixty-Eight Years
text:
In 1922, an American farmer called Charles Osborne was lifting a heavy animal when he fell. He did not seem badly hurt, but soon afterwards he started to hiccup. Most of us hiccup for a few minutes and then forget about it. Osborne, however, did not stop. According to the record books, he hiccupped for about sixty-eight years, until 1990. At first, he hiccupped dozens of times a minute. Later it became slower, but it never really ended. Surprisingly, he lived a fairly normal life. He married twice and had eight children.

His case is extremely rare, but hiccups themselves are something everyone knows. So what actually happens in the body?

Under your lungs there is a large, flat muscle called the diaphragm. Every time you breathe in, it moves down and helps to pull air into your lungs. During a hiccup, this muscle suddenly tightens by itself, without your control. Air rushes into your throat. A fraction of a second later, the vocal cords close quickly and stop the air. This sudden stop makes the familiar "hic" sound.

Many everyday things can start hiccups. Eating too fast, drinking fizzy drinks, swallowing air, laughing a lot or feeling excited or nervous can all play a part. A sudden change in temperature, like hot soup followed by cold water, may also cause them. Doctors believe that these things can irritate the nerves that control the diaphragm.

Then there are the famous cures. Hold your breath. Drink a glass of water upside down. Eat a spoon of sugar. Let someone give you a sudden fright. Almost every family has its own favourite method. The honest truth is that there is very little scientific evidence for most of them. Some may help by changing your breathing or by giving the nerves something else to do. However, ordinary hiccups usually go away by themselves within a few minutes anyway, so it is easy to believe that the cure worked.

One of the biggest mysteries is why we hiccup at all. It does not seem to have any obvious use for adults. Interestingly, babies hiccup a lot, and they even do it before they are born. Some scientists think hiccups may help babies to remove air from their stomachs after feeding. Others suggest that hiccups could be a leftover from our very distant ancestors, who lived in water and had to control how water and air moved through their bodies. Nobody knows for sure yet.

For most people, hiccups are a small, funny problem. If they continue for more than two days, though, doctors advise people to get a medical check. For Charles Osborne, they became a lifelong companion, and a strange place in history.

questions.q: What makes the "hic" sound during a hiccup?
options: The heart beating faster
The stomach pushing food up
The vocal cords closing suddenly and stopping the air
The lungs filling with water
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The vocal cords closing suddenly and stopping the air": diyafram aniden kasılır, hava boğaza dolar ve ses telleri hızla kapanarak "hık" sesini çıkarır.

questions.q: What does the text say about popular hiccup cures?
options: There is little scientific evidence for most of them
Doctors recommend a fright as the best cure
Only sugar really works
They make hiccups last longer
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "There is little scientific evidence for most of them": metne göre bu yöntemlerin çoğunu destekleyen bilimsel kanıt çok azdır; hıçkırık zaten genelde kendiliğinden geçer.

title: A Glue That Did Not Work
text:
In 1968, a chemist called Spencer Silver was working in a laboratory at 3M, a large American company. His job was to create a super-strong glue, the kind that could hold parts of aeroplanes together. One day, he made something very different. His new glue was weak. It stuck to things, but it could be pulled off easily, and it did not leave any marks. Even better, you could stick it again and again.

For most companies, a weak glue sounded like a failure. Silver, however, felt there was something special about it. For several years, he talked about it at meetings and showed it to colleagues. He even suggested a board covered with the glue, where people could stick notes. Nobody was very excited. The glue was "a solution without a problem," as people sometimes say.

The problem finally appeared in a church. Art Fry, another scientist at 3M, sang in a church choir. He used small pieces of paper to mark the songs in his book, but every time he opened it, the papers fell out onto the floor. One Sunday, he remembered Silver's glue. What if his bookmarks had a little of it on the back? They would stay in place, and they would not damage the pages.

Fry made some sticky bookmarks and found that they worked well. Then he noticed something more important. He wrote a question on one of them, stuck it on a report and gave it to his boss. His boss wrote an answer on the same note and gave it back. Suddenly, Fry understood that this was not just a bookmark. It was a new way to communicate.

Even then, success did not come quickly. In 1977, the company tested the product in a few cities, but very few people bought it. Customers did not understand what it was for. So the company tried a new plan. In 1978, it gave away free samples in one city, Boise in the state of Idaho, and let people try them at work. Once office workers used the little notes, most of them wanted more. In 1980, the product was sold across the United States, and soon it spread around the world.

There is also a funny detail about the colour. According to the company, the first notes were yellow simply because the laboratory next door had some spare yellow paper. The colour became so famous that many people still imagine sticky notes as yellow squares.

Today, people use them on fridges, computer screens and walls covered with plans. The story reminds us that a "mistake" is sometimes only an idea waiting for the right problem.

questions.q: What was Spencer Silver originally trying to make?
options: A new kind of paper
Bookmarks for a church
A board for meetings
A very strong glue
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "A very strong glue": uçak parçalarını bir arada tutabilecek süper güçlü bir yapıştırıcı yapmaya çalışıyordu, ama zayıf bir yapıştırıcı ortaya çıktı.

questions.q: Why did the company give away free samples in Boise?
options: Because the yellow paper was cheap there
Because people needed to try the notes to understand them
Because Art Fry lived there
Because the glue was made there
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Because people needed to try the notes to understand them": 1977'deki denemede müşteriler ürünün ne işe yaradığını anlamamıştı; ücretsiz örnekleri kullanınca daha fazlasını istediler.

title: Crows Never Forget a Face
text:
In 2006, a group of researchers at the University of Washington in Seattle did a strange experiment. They put on scary rubber masks, walked onto their university grounds and caught a few wild crows. They put small rings on the birds' legs so they could recognise them later, and then let them go. The birds were not hurt, but they were clearly not happy about it.

What happened next surprised even the scientists. For years afterwards, whenever someone walked across the grounds wearing the same "dangerous" mask, many crows started shouting at them loudly. They flew close and followed the person around. People wearing a different, friendly mask were usually ignored. Even more interesting, crows that had never been caught joined in. Young birds, born after the experiment, also seemed to recognise the dangerous face. The researchers believe the crows had learned from each other who to avoid, and the warning spread through the group.

Crows belong to the same bird family as ravens and magpies, and scientists have long known that these birds are unusually clever. Their brains are small, but their nerve cells are packed tightly together, so they have a lot of thinking power for their size.

On the island of New Caledonia in the Pacific Ocean, wild crows make their own tools. They cut and shape leaves and small sticks, and then use them to pull insects out of holes in trees. Some birds even make hooks at the end of their sticks. In laboratory tests, these crows have solved puzzles with several steps, using one tool to reach another tool, which then reaches the food.

Other experiments seem to come straight from an old story. In one of Aesop's fables, a thirsty crow drops stones into a jar until the water rises high enough to drink. Researchers gave crows a tube of water with a piece of food floating too low to reach. Many of the birds dropped stones into the water, just like in the fable, until the food came up to them.

There are also reports of crows using human technology. In the city of Sendai, in Japan, some crows have been seen placing hard nuts on the road, waiting for cars to drive over them and then collecting the broken pieces. Some even seemed to do it near traffic lights, where they could pick up the food safely while the cars were stopped. Not all scientists agree on how often this really happens, but it is a remarkable idea.

So if a crow is watching you from a tree, be polite. It may remember your face for a very long time, and it might tell its friends about you.

questions.q: What did crows do when they saw the "dangerous" mask?
options: They flew away and never came back
They shouted at the person and followed them
They brought food to the person
They did not react at all
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "They shouted at the person and followed them": "tehlikeli" maskeyi takan kişiye yıllarca bağırdılar, yakından uçup onu takip ettiler.

questions.q: What did crows do in the water tube experiment?
options: They broke the tube with their beaks
They waited for a researcher to help
They dropped stones into the water to raise the food
They used a hook to pull out the tube
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "They dropped stones into the water to raise the food": Ezop masalındaki karga gibi suya taş atıp yiyeceğin yukarı çıkmasını sağladılar.

title: Nobody Wanted the Shopping Trolley
text:
Imagine doing your weekly shopping with only a small basket in your hand. You cannot buy more than you can carry, and your arms soon get tired. In the 1930s, this was normal in American grocery stores. A businessman called Sylvan Goldman, who owned a group of supermarkets in Oklahoma City, noticed the problem. When their baskets became heavy, customers simply stopped shopping and went to pay. For a shop owner, this meant lost sales.

One night in 1936, according to the usual story, Goldman was sitting in his office looking at two folding wooden chairs. He had an idea. What if he put a basket on the seat of a chair, another basket below it and wheels on the legs? Customers could then push their shopping around instead of carrying it. He worked with a mechanic called Fred Young, and together they built a metal frame on wheels that held two baskets. When the shop was closed, the frame could be folded flat and stored in a small space.

In June 1937, Goldman proudly put his new "folding basket carriers" in his stores. He was sure they would be a great success. Instead, almost nobody used them. Men thought that pushing a trolley made them look weak, as if they could not carry a basket. Many women said it reminded them of pushing a baby's pram, and they had pushed enough prams already. Some customers were simply afraid of breaking the strange new machine.

Goldman did not give up. He came up with a clever plan. He hired men and women of different ages to walk around his stores, pushing trolleys and pretending to shop. He also asked a woman at the entrance to offer a trolley to every customer. Slowly, people saw that ordinary shoppers were using them, and they started to try it too. They discovered that the trolleys were very useful. They could buy more food, and their arms did not hurt.

Within a few years, trolleys were spreading to supermarkets across the country, and Goldman became a very rich man. His design also changed the shops themselves. Because customers could now carry more, stores became larger, and car parks grew bigger too.

Later, an inventor called Orla Watson improved the idea. In the late 1940s, he designed a trolley with a back that could swing up, so one trolley could slide into another. This is the design you still see today, with long lines of trolleys pushed together outside the shop.

It is easy to forget that something so ordinary was once new and strange. The shopping trolley needed more than a good idea. It also needed a little help to change people's minds.

questions.q: Why did customers not use the trolleys at first?
options: They were too expensive to use
They were often broken
Shops did not have enough space for them
People felt strange or embarrassed pushing them
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "People felt strange or embarrassed pushing them": erkekler zayıf görüneceklerini, kadınlar ise bebek arabası ittiklerini düşündü; bazıları da bu garip makineyi kırmaktan korktu.

questions.q: How did Goldman change people's minds?
options: He paid people to push trolleys around the store
He made the baskets smaller
He gave free food to shoppers
He sold trolleys to customers
