title: Why Do Our Fingers Wrinkle in the Bath?
text:
After a long bath or a swim in the sea, you look at your hands and see something funny. The skin on your fingers and toes has become wrinkly, a bit like a raisin. For many years, most people had a simple explanation for this. They thought the outer layer of skin took in water, became bigger and folded, just like a piece of paper that gets wet. It sounds reasonable, but the real story seems to be more surprising.

The first clue came from hospitals. In the 1930s, doctors noticed that when certain nerves in a patient's hand were cut or damaged, the fingers did not wrinkle in water any more. If wrinkles were only caused by water, the nerves should not matter at all. This suggested that the body itself was controlling the process. Later research confirmed this. When our fingers stay in water, the nervous system tells the small blood vessels under the skin to become narrower. The tissue under the skin gets slightly smaller, and the skin on top is pulled into folds.

So wrinkly fingers are not an accident. They are an active response. But why would the body do this? What could the purpose be?

In 2011, a scientist called Mark Changizi and his colleagues suggested an answer. They noticed that the wrinkles often form patterns that look like rivers or the treads on car tyres. Tyre treads help to push water away, so the tyre can grip a wet road. Perhaps wrinkly fingers do the same thing. They might help our hands and feet hold on to wet rocks, wet branches or wet food.

Two years later, a team at Newcastle University in England tested this idea. They asked volunteers to move small objects, such as marbles, from one box to another. Some of the objects were wet and some were dry. People with wrinkly fingers moved the wet objects faster than people with smooth fingers. With dry objects, there was no difference. This seemed to support the grip idea.

However, science rarely ends with one experiment. Other research teams tried similar tests and did not find the same clear result. Some scientists also point out that many other animals that live near water do not get wrinkly fingers. So the question is still open, and researchers continue to study it.

What we do know is that the wrinkles are harmless and temporary. When you leave the water and dry your hands, the blood vessels relax, and the skin becomes smooth again, usually within half an hour. And in a way, wrinkly fingers can be useful even for doctors. Because they depend on working nerves, a simple water test can sometimes help to check whether the nerves in a hand are healthy.

Next time you get out of the bath, take a moment to look at your fingertips. You may be looking at a small piece of ancient engineering.

questions.q: What did doctors notice about patients with damaged nerves in their hands?
options: Their fingers wrinkled faster
Their fingers did not wrinkle in water
Their fingers became very dry
Their fingers changed colour
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Their fingers did not wrinkle in water": elindeki sinirleri hasar görmüş hastaların parmakları suda buruşmuyordu; bu, buruşmayı vücudun kontrol ettiğini gösterdi.

questions.q: What is the current situation of the "grip" idea?
options: It has been completely proved
All scientists reject it
It is supported by some studies, but scientists still disagree
It was never tested
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "It is supported by some studies, but scientists still disagree": Newcastle deneyi fikri destekledi, ama başka ekipler aynı sonucu bulamadı; soru hâlâ açık.

title: The Secret Voices of Elephants
text:
In 1984, an American scientist called Katy Payne was visiting a zoo in Portland, Oregon. She was standing near the elephants when she felt something odd. The air seemed to shake gently, like the deep sound of a church organ that you feel in your chest more than you hear with your ears. Payne had spent years studying the songs of whales, so she was used to listening carefully. She began to wonder: were the elephants talking to each other in sounds too low for humans to hear?

She came back with special recording equipment. When she played the recordings faster, the hidden sounds became audible. She was right. Elephants were producing deep calls, now known as rumbles, many of them below the lowest note that human ears can catch. Sounds like these are called infrasound.

Low sounds have a special advantage. They lose less energy as they travel, so they can go much further than high sounds. Researchers working in Africa later showed that elephant rumbles may travel several kilometres, especially in the cool, still air of early evening. This could help families that are far apart to stay in contact, to find each other or to warn others of danger.

There may even be another way of listening. Some scientists believe elephants can feel these sounds through the ground. Their large feet contain many sensitive nerve endings, and some studies suggest that they can pick up vibrations that travel through the earth. Elephants have sometimes been seen standing very still, with one foot lifted slightly, as if they were listening through their feet. This idea is still being researched, but it is a fascinating possibility.

Elephant conversations also seem to be very rich. Families greet each other with loud rumbles and touching trunks when they meet again after a separation. Mothers and their babies have their own calls. In 2024, a team of researchers studying wild elephants in Kenya published a surprising result. Using a computer program, they found that some calls seemed to be directed at particular elephants. When the researchers played a recording of a call that was aimed at one elephant, that animal often reacted more strongly than when it heard calls aimed at others. The team suggested that elephants might use something like names for each other. Other scientists say more work is needed, but if it is true, it would be very rare in the animal world.

Elephants are social and intelligent animals, and they live in large family groups led by an older female. Understanding their hidden voices may also help to protect them. If people know how elephants communicate, they can plan roads, farms and parks that disturb them less.

It is humbling to think that all around those great animals, there are conversations going on that we cannot hear. We just need the right tools, and a little patience, to listen.

questions.q: Why can elephant rumbles travel so far?
options: Elephants shout very loudly during the day
The wind always carries them
They travel only through water
Low sounds lose less energy as they travel
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Low sounds lose less energy as they travel": alçak sesler yolculuk sırasında daha az enerji kaybeder, bu yüzden kilometrelerce uzağa gidebilir.

questions.q: What did the 2024 study in Kenya suggest?
options: Elephants cannot hear infrasound
Elephants only talk to their mothers
Elephants forget each other after a separation
Elephants might use something like names for each other
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Elephants might use something like names for each other": bazı çağrılar belirli fillere yönelikti ve o filler kendi çağrılarına daha güçlü tepki verdi.

title: The Ring on the Ferry
text:
Every morning at half past seven, Selin took the ferry from Kadıköy to Karaköy. She liked the short trip across the water. She drank her tea, fed bread to the seagulls and watched the city wake up. For twenty minutes, nobody asked her for anything.

One grey Tuesday in November, something went wrong. When she reached her office, she looked down at her hand and her heart stopped. Her ring was gone. It was a thin gold ring with a small blue stone, and it had belonged to her grandmother. Her grandmother had given it to her on her eighteenth birthday and had said, “Never take it off, and it will always bring you home.”

Selin searched her bag, her pockets and her coat. She walked back to the ferry station and looked on the ground. She asked the man at the ticket office, but he only shook his head. “Lost things usually go to the main office,” he said kindly. “But a ring is very small, my dear.”

That evening, she could not eat. She called her mother, who tried to make her feel better. “Rings get lost,” her mother said. “Your grandmother lost her keys every single week, you know. She would laugh at all this.” Selin smiled a little, but she still felt empty.

The next morning, she took the same ferry. She did not drink tea or feed the seagulls. She walked up and down the lower deck, looking under every seat. An old man with a large white moustache was watching her. He sold simit on the ferry, and Selin had bought from him perhaps a hundred times, but she had never really talked to him.

“You are looking for something,” he said. It was not a question.

“A ring,” she answered. “Gold, with a blue stone. I think I lost it yesterday.”

The old man put down his tray. He reached into the pocket of his jacket and took out a small paper bag. Inside the bag, wrapped in a clean napkin, was her ring.

“It was between two seats,” he said. “I saw it when I was cleaning up the sesame seeds. I knew it was yours, because you always turn it round and round when you look at the water. I waited for you yesterday evening, but you took a different boat.”

Selin did not know what to say. She wanted to hug him, but instead she tried to pay him. He refused at once. “Buy two simit tomorrow,” he said, “and we are even.”

From that day, Selin bought two simit every morning. She ate one and gave the other to the seagulls. And sometimes, on quiet mornings, she sat with the old simit seller and listened to his stories about the ferries of forty years ago. Her grandmother had been right after all. The ring had brought her home, and it had also brought her a new friend.

questions.q: Why was the ring so important to Selin?
options: It was very expensive.
It had belonged to her grandmother.
Her boyfriend had given it to her.
She had bought it on the ferry.
questions.explain: Yüzük babaannesinden/anneannesinden kalmıştı: "It had belonged to her grandmother." Bu yüzden Selin için çok değerliydi.

questions.q: How did the simit seller know the ring was Selin's?
options: Her name was written inside it.
The ticket office told him.
He had seen her turning it while she looked at the water.
Selin had shown him a photo of it.
questions.explain: Simitçi, Selin'in denize bakarken yüzüğünü hep çevirdiğini görmüştü; doğru cevap "He had seen her turning it while she looked at the water."

title: My First Job at the Bakery
text:
When I was sixteen, I wanted a bicycle more than anything in the world. My parents said I could have one if I paid for half of it myself. So in the summer holiday, I found my first job at a small bakery near our flat in İzmir.

The bakery belonged to a man everyone called Usta Hamit. He was short and round, with arms as strong as a wrestler’s. On the first day, he looked at me for a long time and said, “Can you wake up at four in the morning?” I said yes, although I had never woken up before seven in my whole life.

The next morning, my alarm rang at four. It was completely dark outside, and the streets were silent. When I arrived, the bakery was already warm and full of light. Usta Hamit gave me a white apron and showed me the ovens, the flour and the long wooden tables. “Today you will only watch,” he said. “Bread does not like people who hurry.”

I watched him mix flour, water, salt and yeast. I watched him push and fold the dough with his big hands, again and again, until it was smooth and soft. He never looked at a clock, but he always knew when the bread was ready. “You must listen to it,” he told me. “Good bread sounds hollow when you knock on it.”

By the third day, I was allowed to shape the loaves. My first ones looked terrible. Some were flat, some were too fat and one looked like a sleeping cat. I was sure Usta Hamit would be angry. Instead, he laughed so loudly that the windows shook. Then he put my strange loaves in the oven with the others.

“Who will buy these?” I asked.

“Someone always buys the ugly ones,” he said. “They taste exactly the same.”

He was right. At seven o’clock, the customers began to arrive: workers on their way to the port, mothers with small children, a retired teacher who wanted his bread “not too dark, not too light”. A little boy pointed at my cat-shaped loaf and shouted, “I want that one!” His mother paid for it with a smile, and I felt prouder than I had ever felt at school.

The summer passed quickly. My hands became stronger and my loaves became rounder. I learned to carry heavy bags of flour, to keep the floor clean and to say good morning to every customer, even the grumpy ones. Most importantly, I learned that hard work feels different when someone trusts you.

In September, I bought my bicycle. It was blue and shiny, and I rode it everywhere. But the first place I rode to was the bakery. Usta Hamit came outside, wiped the flour from his hands and examined the bicycle very seriously.

“Good,” he said at last. “Now you can deliver bread too.”

I worked there every summer until I finished school. Even now, many years later, I cannot walk past a bakery at dawn without smiling.

questions.q: Why did the narrator take a job at the bakery?
options: To pay for half of a bicycle.
Because his school asked him to.
To learn how to become a cook.
Because Usta Hamit was his uncle.
questions.explain: Anlatıcı, ailesinin şartı yüzünden bisikletin yarısını ödemek için çalıştı: "To pay for half of a bicycle."

questions.q: What happened to the narrator's strange, cat-shaped loaf?
options: Usta Hamit threw it away.
The narrator ate it himself.
It burned in the oven.
A little boy chose it and his mother bought it.
questions.explain: Küçük bir çocuk kedi şeklindeki ekmeği istedi ve annesi satın aldı: "A little boy chose it and his mother bought it."

title: Grandfather's Radio
text:
In the corner of my grandfather’s living room in Konya, there was an old wooden radio. It was as big as a suitcase and had two round buttons, one for the volume and one for the stations. Nobody was allowed to touch it except my grandfather.

Every evening after dinner, he sat in his chair, turned on the radio and listened to the news. Then he listened to old songs and closed his eyes. My cousins and I thought the radio was boring. We had phones and tablets, and we could listen to anything we wanted. Why did he need that heavy old box?

One summer, when I was twelve, the radio stopped working. My grandfather turned the buttons again and again, but there was only silence. He did not say much, but for the next few days he looked tired and sad. My grandmother told me quietly, “That radio is older than your father. It has a story.”

I asked my grandfather to tell me the story. At first, he waved his hand and said it was not important. But that night, on the balcony, under a sky full of stars, he finally began.

“In 1965, I was a young man,” he said. “I worked in a small repair shop in the city. I fixed shoes, bags, umbrellas, anything. One day, a farmer came in with this radio. It was broken, and he could not pay for the repair. He said, ‘Keep it. Maybe one day you can make it work.’”

My grandfather spent every evening for three months on that radio. He had no books and no teacher, only patience. He opened it, studied every wire and asked questions to anyone who knew a little about electricity. Finally, one cold winter night, the radio made a sound. Then a voice came out of it, singing an old song.

“At that exact moment,” my grandfather said, “your grandmother walked into the shop to collect her father’s shoes. She heard the music and stopped at the door. She asked me what the song was. I didn’t know, so I invited her to stay and listen until the end.”

I stared at him. “So the radio is the reason you met Grandma?”

He laughed. “The radio, and her father’s old shoes.”

The next day, I made a plan. My friend’s uncle, Mr Ferit, repaired old electronic things in a small shop near the market. I carried the radio there with my cousin. It was so heavy that we had to stop every few minutes. Mr Ferit opened the back, looked inside and smiled. “Only one small part,” he said. “Come back on Friday.”

On Friday evening, we put the radio back in its corner. We did not say anything to my grandfather. After dinner, he sat in his chair as usual and turned the button without hope. Suddenly, music filled the room.

It was the same old song. My grandfather looked at my grandmother, and she looked at him, and for a moment nobody spoke. Then he held out his hand, and they danced slowly in the middle of the living room while we watched from the door.

questions.q: How did the grandfather get the radio in 1965?
options: He bought it in a big shop.
His father gave it to him.
A farmer who could not pay for the repair left it with him.
He found it in the street.
questions.explain: Tamir parasını ödeyemeyen bir çiftçi radyoyu ona bıraktı: "A farmer who could not pay for the repair left it with him."

questions.q: What did the narrator do to surprise the grandparents?
options: Bought them a new radio.
Took the radio to Mr Ferit to be repaired.
Played the old song on a phone.
Wrote a letter about their story.
questions.explain: Anlatıcı radyoyu tamir için Ferit Bey'e götürdü: "Took the radio to Mr Ferit to be repaired." Böylece eski şarkı yeniden çaldı.

title: A Student in Lisbon
text:
When Deniz arrived in Lisbon for her exchange semester, she knew exactly three words of Portuguese: hello, thank you and coffee. She had studied English for years, so she was not worried about her classes. She was worried about everything else.

Her room was at the top of an old building in a neighbourhood full of narrow streets and steep hills. The walls were covered with blue and white tiles, and from her small window she could see the river. It was beautiful, but on the first night she felt very far from home. She ate a sandwich alone on her bed and called her mother for an hour.

The next morning, she went out to buy bread. The woman in the little shop downstairs was about seventy, with short silver hair and bright glasses. She said something quickly in Portuguese. Deniz smiled and said, “Obrigada,” which means thank you. The woman laughed and said something else. Deniz said, “Obrigada,” again. It was the only word she could think of.

This happened every morning for a week. Deniz bought bread, the woman talked and Deniz thanked her. One day, the woman finally pointed at herself and said slowly, “Dona Graça.” Then she pointed at Deniz with a question in her eyes.

“Deniz,” said Deniz. “It means sea in Turkish.”

Dona Graça did not understand the words, but she understood the gesture when Deniz pointed towards the river. Her face lit up. “Mar!” she said. “Deniz, mar!” From that moment, she called her “Menina Mar”, the sea girl.

After that, the morning visits became small lessons. Dona Graça taught her the names of the breads and cakes. She corrected her pronunciation patiently and clapped when Deniz got something right. In return, Deniz taught her a few Turkish words. Dona Graça especially liked “afiyet olsun”, which she said very seriously to every customer, even though none of them understood.

At university, things were also getting easier. Deniz joined a group of students from Brazil, Poland and Italy. They studied together in the library and explored the city at weekends. They rode the famous yellow trams up the hills, tried grilled sardines at a summer festival and got lost so many times that it became a joke.

In December, Deniz had a bad cold and stayed in bed for three days. On the second day, someone knocked on her door. It was Dona Graça, holding a pot of hot soup. She had climbed four floors of stairs with it. “Canja,” she said, a chicken soup with rice. It tasted almost exactly like the soup Deniz’s grandmother made at home.

When the semester ended, Deniz could hold a simple conversation in Portuguese. On her last morning, she went down to the shop to say goodbye. She had practised a short speech all night, but when she saw Dona Graça, she forgot every word. They just hugged for a long time.

Now Deniz is back in Ankara. Every few weeks, she receives a postcard from Lisbon with a picture of the river. It always ends with the same two words, written in careful Turkish letters: “Afiyet olsun.”

questions.q: Why did Dona Graça call Deniz "Menina Mar"?
options: Because Deniz could swim very well.
Because Deniz lived near the beach.
Because Deniz's name means sea in Turkish.
Because Deniz always wore blue clothes.
questions.explain: Deniz adının Türkçede "sea" anlamına geldiğini anlatınca ona bu ad takıldı: "Because Deniz's name means sea in Turkish."

questions.q: What did Dona Graça do when Deniz was ill?
options: She brought her a pot of chicken soup.
She called a doctor.
She sent a postcard to her mother.
She closed her shop for three days.
questions.explain: Graça Hanım dört kat merdiven çıkıp sıcak tavuk çorbası getirdi: "She brought her a pot of chicken soup."

title: The Mystery of the Missing Slippers
text:
In our apartment building in Eskişehir, everyone leaves their shoes and slippers outside the door. It is an old habit, and nobody ever thought about it twice. Then, one spring, the slippers started to disappear.

First, Mrs Nermin on the second floor lost one pink slipper. Only one. She looked everywhere and finally decided that her grandson had taken it as a joke. A week later, Mr Orhan on the fourth floor lost a brown leather slipper. Again, only one. Then my little brother lost one of his blue football slippers, and that was when I decided to investigate.

I was eleven years old, and I had read every detective story in our school library. I took a notebook and a pencil and made a list. Who had lost a slipper? When? Which floor? I interviewed every family in the building. Some of them laughed at me, but most of them were happy to help. Mr Orhan even gave me a biscuit and called me “Inspector”.

My list showed something interesting. All the slippers had disappeared at night, and all of them were soft ones. Nobody had lost a hard shoe or a boot. I also noticed that the doors on the top floor had never lost anything.

My first suspect was Kerem, the teenager from the third floor, because he always looked bored. But when I asked him, he was so surprised that I knew he was innocent. My second suspect was the wind. However, the wind cannot carry a slipper up the stairs, and two slippers had been found later on the stairs between the fourth and fifth floors.

So I decided to watch. On Friday night, I told my parents I was going to bed early. Instead, I sat by our door with a torch and my notebook. I waited and waited. At about half past one, I was almost asleep when I heard a soft sound. Something was moving on the stairs.

I opened the door a little and turned on my torch. There, in the middle of the landing, was a small grey cat. In her mouth, she was carrying Mrs Nermin’s second pink slipper. She looked at me with big yellow eyes, as if I was the one doing something wrong. Then she ran up the stairs.

I followed her very quietly to the top floor. Next to the door to the roof, there was a small space behind an old cupboard. Inside, on a pile of slippers, were four tiny kittens, warm and sleeping. The mother cat had built them a bed.

The next morning, I called a meeting of the whole building. I showed everyone my notebook and then led them up to the top floor. When they saw the kittens, nobody was angry anymore. Mrs Nermin said the cat could keep her slippers. Mr Orhan brought a proper basket and an old blanket.

When the kittens were bigger, three of them found homes in our building. The fourth one lives with us now. We call her Inspector, and she still loves slippers.

questions.q: What did the narrator notice in the list of lost slippers?
options: They all belonged to children.
They were all soft and lost at night.
They were all lost on the second floor.
They were all new.
questions.explain: Listede tüm terliklerin yumuşak olduğu ve gece kaybolduğu görülüyordu: "They were all soft and lost at night."

questions.q: Why was the cat taking the slippers?
options: She liked to play with them in the street.
Kerem had trained her to do it.
She wanted to eat the leather.
She was making a bed for her kittens.
questions.explain: Anne kedi yavruları için terliklerden yatak yapıyordu: "She was making a bed for her kittens."

title: The Wrong Bus
text:
Tolga had planned his holiday for months. He was going to visit his old university friend Burak, who now lived in a small town on the Aegean coast. Burak had sent him a long message with clear directions: take the night bus from Ankara, change buses in the city centre, and get off at the last stop.

Everything went well until the second bus. Tolga was tired after the long night, and the bus station was crowded and noisy. He saw a bus with the right number on the front, jumped on and fell asleep almost immediately.

When he woke up, the sea was nowhere. Instead, he saw mountains, olive trees and a narrow road climbing higher and higher. He checked his phone, but there was no signal. He went to the driver and showed him Burak’s message. The driver read it, then laughed so hard that he had to stop the bus.

“Wrong direction, my friend,” he said. “Same number, different company. This bus goes to the villages in the mountains.”

The next bus back would come in the evening. The driver left Tolga in a tiny village square with a fountain, a mosque, a teahouse and a sleeping dog. Five old men were sitting outside the teahouse, playing backgammon. They all stopped and looked at him.

Tolga explained his problem. Within minutes, the whole village seemed to know about the lost young man from Ankara. Someone brought him tea. Someone else brought bread, cheese and tomatoes from a garden. One of the old men, Hüseyin Amca, invited him to watch the backgammon game, and then to play.

Tolga was a terrible player, and everyone enjoyed this very much. They gave him advice, argued about his moves and laughed at his mistakes. After he lost three games in a row, Hüseyin Amca patted him on the back. “Do not worry,” he said. “In our village, losing is also a kind of skill.”

In the afternoon, a woman took him to see the old stone houses and a waterfall behind the village. From the top of the hill, he could see the whole valley, green and gold in the sunlight. Far away, there was a thin blue line. It was the sea, the place he was supposed to be.

He finally found a little signal near the waterfall and called Burak. Burak was worried at first, then he could not stop laughing. “Stay there,” he said. “I know that village. I am coming with the car.”

When Burak arrived, the old men insisted that he should play backgammon too. He was even worse than Tolga. By the time the two friends left, it was dark, and they had two bags of figs, a jar of honey and an invitation to a wedding the next month.

Tolga spent a wonderful week by the sea, swimming, eating fish and talking with Burak late into the night. But when people asked him about his holiday, he always told the same story first. It was the story of the wrong bus, which took him exactly where he needed to go.

questions.q: Why did Tolga get on the wrong bus?
options: Burak gave him the wrong number.
It had the same number but belonged to a different company.
He could not read the sign in the dark.
The driver told him it was the right bus.
questions.explain: Otobüsün numarası aynıydı ama başka bir firmaya aitti: "It had the same number but belonged to a different company."

questions.q: How did the villagers treat Tolga?
options: They ignored him.
They asked him to pay for the tea.
They sent him away quickly.
They gave him food, played backgammon with him and showed him around.
questions.explain: Köylüler ona yiyecek verdi, tavla oynattı ve köyü gezdirdi: "They gave him food, played backgammon with him and showed him around."

title: A Letter After Twenty Years
text:
When Elif was ten years old, her teacher, Mrs Aydan, gave the class an unusual homework task. “Write a letter to yourself,” she said. “Not to the person you are now, but to the person you will be in twenty years. Tell her about your life, your dreams and your best friends. I will keep the letters, and one day I will send them to you.”

The children laughed. Twenty years seemed like forever. But they all wrote their letters, put them in envelopes and wrote their names on the front. Mrs Aydan put the envelopes in a large brown box, and the class forgot about them almost immediately.

Twenty years later, Elif was living in Bursa. She worked as a nurse at a busy hospital, and her days were long and tiring. One evening, she came home and found an envelope among the bills. The handwriting on the front was round and childish. It was her own.

Inside, there was a short note from Mrs Aydan, now retired. “I promised,” it said. “Here is your letter. I hope life has been kind to you.” And under the note, there was a page from an old school notebook, covered in pencil and small drawings of stars.

Elif sat down at the kitchen table and began to read.

“Dear Elif,” the letter said. “I hope you are a famous singer now. If you are not a singer, I hope you are a doctor or a vet. Do you still have long hair? Do you still hate aubergines? My best friend is Zeynep. We are going to be friends forever. We have a secret club, and the password is ‘purple banana’. Please say hello to Zeynep from me.”

Elif laughed out loud. She was not a famous singer. She was not a doctor or a vet, but she was a nurse, which felt close enough. Her hair was short now, and she actually loved aubergines. But when she read Zeynep’s name, she stopped laughing.

She and Zeynep had been inseparable for years. Then Zeynep’s family moved to Germany when they were fourteen. They wrote to each other for a while, then sent messages, and then, slowly, nothing. Elif could not even remember who had stopped writing first.

That night, she could not sleep. At midnight, she got up and searched for Zeynep online. It took a long time. There were many women with the same name. But finally she found a photo of a woman with the same bright smile, standing in front of a small bookshop in Hamburg.

Elif wrote a message, deleted it and wrote it again. In the end, she sent only two words: “Purple banana?”

The answer came the next morning. It was a voice message, and for the first ten seconds there was only laughter. Then Zeynep said, “I have been waiting for that password for sixteen years.”

They talked for three hours that weekend. In the summer, Zeynep came to Bursa with her husband and her two daughters. The two women sat on Elif’s balcony until late at night, eating aubergines and making plans. Before Zeynep left, they both wrote a new letter, to be opened in another twenty years.

questions.q: What did Mrs Aydan ask the children to do?
options: Write a letter to their future selves.
Write a letter to a friend in Germany.
Draw a picture of their best friend.
Learn a secret password.
questions.explain: Öğretmen çocuklardan yirmi yıl sonraki kendilerine mektup yazmalarını istedi: "Write a letter to their future selves."

questions.q: Why did Elif send the words "Purple banana?"
options: It was the name of Zeynep's bookshop.
It was a joke about her favourite food.

Mrs Aydan told her to write it.
questions.explain: "Purple banana" çocukken kurdukları gizli kulübün şifresiydi: "It was the password of their old secret club."

title: The Yellow Umbrella
text:
Mert was not a lucky person, or that was what he believed. He missed buses by a few seconds. His toast always fell on the floor butter side down. And on the day of his most important job interview, it began to rain heavily in Ankara.

He had no umbrella. He stood in the doorway of a small shop and looked at his watch. The interview was in forty minutes, on the other side of Kızılay. If he walked, his only good suit would be completely wet. If he waited, he would be late.

Next to him in the doorway stood an elderly woman with a bright yellow umbrella. She noticed his worried face and asked where he was going. When he explained, she simply handed him the umbrella.

“Take it,” she said. “I live just there, across the road. I am not going anywhere today.”

Mert refused at first, but she insisted. “Bring it back one day if you want,” she said. “Flat number six, the green door. If you do not bring it back, it does not matter. Umbrellas are like luck. They move from person to person.”

He thanked her many times and ran. The yellow umbrella was so bright that people turned to look at him. He arrived at the office two minutes early, dry except for his shoes. In the waiting room, there were four other candidates, all looking serious in dark suits. Mert put the yellow umbrella next to his chair and tried to stay calm.

The interview went better than he expected. Near the end, the manager, a tall woman with grey hair, smiled and pointed at the umbrella. “I saw you from the window,” she said. “That is the brightest umbrella I have seen in years. Where did you get it?”

Mert told her the whole story: the rain, the doorway, the old woman and the green door. The manager listened carefully, and she laughed when he repeated the old woman’s words about luck. The interview, which had been formal until then, became a friendly conversation.

A week later, Mert received a phone call. He had got the job. The manager told him that many candidates had the right qualifications, but he was the only one who had told an honest, interesting story. “In this job, you will speak to customers all day,” she said. “I need someone people want to listen to.”

That evening, Mert bought a box of chocolates and went to the green door. He rang the bell of flat number six, holding the yellow umbrella. The old woman, whose name was Mrs Saadet, invited him in for tea. She was delighted with his news. They talked for an hour about her late husband, about Mert’s family and about the city before all the tall buildings.

When he tried to give back the umbrella, she shook her head. “Keep it,” she said. “But remember what I told you.”

Mert still has the yellow umbrella. He no longer thinks he is unlucky. And last winter, when he saw a young student standing in the rain outside his office, he did not hesitate for a second.

questions.q: Why did the manager give Mert the job?
options: He had the best qualifications of all.
He arrived earlier than everyone else.
He told an honest and interesting story.
Mrs Saadet was her mother.
questions.explain: Müdür, Mert'in dürüst ve ilginç bir hikâye anlattığını söyledi: "He told an honest and interesting story."

questions.q: What did Mert do at the end of the story?
options: He threw away the umbrella.
He sold the umbrella to a student.
He bought a new umbrella for Mrs Saadet.
He was ready to give the umbrella to a student in the rain.
questions.explain: Yağmurda bekleyen öğrenciyi görünce hiç tereddüt etmedi; yani şemsiyeyi ona verecekti: "He was ready to give the umbrella to a student in the rain."

title: The Village Girls' Football Team
text:
In a small village in central Anatolia, there was a school with one football, one dusty field and forty-two students. For as long as anyone could remember, only the boys played football at break time. The girls watched from the wall or played their own games in the corner.

Then a new teacher arrived. Her name was Miss Gülay, and she came from a big city. On her first day, she stood by the field and watched the boys play. Then she turned to the girls on the wall and asked, “Why aren’t you playing?”

The girls looked at each other. “Football is for boys,” said a girl called Esra. Everyone nodded.

Miss Gülay smiled. “I played football until I was twenty,” she said. “I was the goalkeeper of my university team. Tomorrow, bring your trainers.”

The next day, nine girls came with trainers. Some of their mothers had been surprised, and a few of their fathers had laughed, but nobody had said no. Miss Gülay taught them how to pass, how to stop the ball and how to run without getting tired too quickly. The first training sessions were a disaster. The girls kicked the air instead of the ball, fell over and laughed so much that they could hardly stand up.

But they came back every day. Slowly, they got better. Esra turned out to be very fast. A quiet girl named Fadime, who never spoke in class, was fearless in goal. Even the boys started to stop their own game to watch.

In April, Miss Gülay had an idea. There was a football tournament for village schools in the nearest town. Normally, only boys’ teams took part. She wrote to the organisers and asked if a girls’ team could join. After two weeks, the answer came: yes, but they had to play against the boys’ teams, because there were no other girls’ teams.

The girls were nervous, but they agreed. The whole village helped. The women sewed red shirts with numbers on the back. The man who owned the village shop paid for new socks. On the day of the tournament, a small bus took the team to town, and half the village followed in tractors and cars.

Their first match was against a strong school team. The boys smiled when they saw the girls, but they stopped smiling after ten minutes, when Esra ran past three defenders and scored. The village supporters made so much noise that a few birds left the trees. The girls lost the match three to two, but nobody felt like a loser.

In the second match, Fadime stopped two penalties, and the girls won one to nothing. In the end, they finished third in the tournament. On the way home, the whole bus sang songs, and the bus driver sang the loudest.

Today, the village school has two footballs, a new net and a mixed team. At break time, boys and girls play together. And on the wall of the school, there is a photograph of nine girls in red shirts, holding a small bronze cup and smiling at the camera.

questions.q: Why did the girls not play football before Miss Gülay came?
options: The school had no football.
They thought football was only for boys.
Their teacher did not allow it.
The field was too small.
questions.explain: Kızlar futbolun yalnızca erkekler için olduğunu düşünüyordu: "They thought football was only for boys."

questions.q: How did the girls' team do in the tournament?
options: They won every match.
They lost every match.
They did not play because there were no other girls' teams.
They finished third.
questions.explain: Takım turnuvayı üçüncü olarak bitirdi: "They finished third."

title: Grandmother's Secret Recipe
text:
Everyone in our family agreed on one thing: nobody made stuffed peppers like Grandmother Hatice. Her peppers were soft but not too soft, and the rice inside was full of flavour. At every family dinner, the plate was empty in minutes, and my uncles always argued about who could take the last one.

Many people had asked for her recipe. My mother had asked. My aunts had asked. Even our neighbour, who was a professional cook, had asked. Every time, my grandmother gave the same answer with a mysterious smile: “There is a secret ingredient, and I will tell it only to the right person.”

When I was fourteen, I decided I wanted to be the right person. I started spending Saturday mornings at her house. At first, she did not let me cook. I washed the vegetables, cleaned the table and listened to her stories about her childhood in a village near Malatya. She told me about the apricot trees, the cold winters and the big pots of food her mother made for weddings.

After a few weeks, she let me cut onions. I cried a lot, and she laughed a lot. Later, she taught me to wash the rice until the water was clear, to cut the tops of the peppers carefully and to use fresh mint, not dry mint. I wrote everything in a small notebook. Onions, rice, tomatoes, mint, black pepper, a little sugar, olive oil. I watched her hands very carefully. I was sure that one day I would see her add something special when she thought I was not looking.

But I never saw it. Her ingredients were the same as everyone else’s. When I tried to make the peppers at home, using my notebook, they were good, but they were not hers. My family ate them politely, but my uncles did not argue about the last one.

I went back to my grandmother, a little disappointed. “I did everything you did,” I said. “What is the secret ingredient? Please tell me now.”

She looked at me for a long time. Then she took my hands, which smelled of onions, and said, “You already know it. You just have not noticed.”

I did not understand. So she explained. When she cooked, she never hurried. She cooked the onions slowly until they were sweet. She let the rice rest. She cooked the peppers on a very low heat for a long time, and she never lifted the lid to look. “Most people are too busy,” she said. “They want everything quickly. The secret is time, and a little love for the people who will eat it.”

I thought this was just something old people say. But the next time I cooked the peppers, I did it her way. I did not look at my phone. I did not turn up the heat. I waited.

That evening, at the family dinner, the plate was empty in minutes. My uncles argued about the last pepper. And from the other end of the table, my grandmother looked at me and gave me her mysterious smile.

questions.q: What happened when the narrator first cooked the peppers at home?
options: They were good, but not as good as Grandmother's.
They burned completely.
Everyone said they were better than Grandmother's.
Nobody wanted to eat them.
questions.explain: Dolmalar iyiydi ama babaanneninki gibi değildi: "They were good, but not as good as Grandmother's."

questions.q: What was the real secret ingredient?
options: A special kind of sugar.
Dry mint from Malatya.
Time and love for the people who eat the food.
A spice that nobody could see.
questions.explain: Babaanne sırrın zaman ve yemeği yiyecek insanlara duyulan sevgi olduğunu söyledi: "Time and love for the people who eat the food."

title: From Savur to Stockholm
text:
In October 2015, a phone call woke up a Turkish scientist in North Carolina early in the morning. The caller was from Stockholm, and the news was extraordinary: Aziz Sancar had won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He shared it with two other scientists, Tomas Lindahl and Paul Modrich, for their work on how cells repair damaged DNA.

His story began far from any modern laboratory. He was born in 1946 in Savur, a small town in Mardin, in south-eastern Turkey. He was the seventh of eight children in a farming family. His parents could not read or write, but they believed strongly in education and made sure their children went to school. Young Aziz was a hard-working student, and his teachers encouraged him to continue.

He studied medicine at Istanbul University and graduated in 1969. Afterwards, he went back to his home region and worked for a while as a doctor in Savur. Treating patients was meaningful work, but he kept asking deeper questions. Why do cells become ill? How does life protect itself? He realised that he wanted to understand the basic chemistry of life, so he decided to become a researcher.

He moved to the United States and completed a doctorate at the University of Texas at Dallas. His subject was an enzyme called photolyase. Our DNA, the long molecule that carries genetic information, is damaged every day by ultraviolet light from the sun. Some living things, such as bacteria, have photolyase, which uses the energy of blue light to repair this damage. Sancar wanted to know exactly how this tiny machine worked.

The early years were not easy. At one point he could not find a job in research and had to work as a laboratory technician. He did not give up. Later, at the University of North Carolina, he and his team discovered another, more complex system that cells use to cut out damaged pieces of DNA and replace them with correct copies. This process, which scientists call nucleotide excision repair, is extremely important in human cells, too. When it does not work, people can become very sensitive to sunlight and have a much higher risk of skin cancer.

His research also helped to explain how our internal "body clock" works, and why some cancer treatments may work better at certain times of the day. These ideas could one day make medical treatments both safer and more effective.

Sancar has always kept close ties with Turkey. Together with his wife, Gwen, who is also a scientist, he opened a house near the university in North Carolina to support Turkish students and researchers. After he received the Nobel Prize, he placed his medal at Anıtkabir in Ankara, saying that it belonged to his country.

When young people ask him for advice, he usually talks about hard work and patience rather than genius. His own journey, from a small town in Mardin to the stage in Stockholm, is perhaps the best example of what he means.

questions.q: Why did Aziz Sancar stop working as a doctor?
options: He wanted to understand the basic chemistry of life.
He could not find patients in Savur.
His parents asked him to move abroad.
He wanted to become a teacher.
questions.explain: Metne göre hasta tedavi etmek anlamlıydı ama o, yaşamın temel kimyasını anlamak istediğini fark etti ve araştırmacı olmaya karar verdi. Doğru cevap "He wanted to understand the basic chemistry of life."

questions.q: What did Sancar do with his Nobel medal?
options: He sold it to support students.
He gave it to his university in Texas.
He placed it at Anıtkabir in Ankara.
He kept it in his laboratory.
questions.explain: Nobel madalyasını, ülkesine ait olduğunu söyleyerek Ankara'daki Anıtkabir'e bıraktı. Doğru cevap "He placed it at Anıtkabir in Ankara."

title: The First Programmer
text:
Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815, and she was the only legitimate child of the famous poet Lord Byron. She never really knew her father. Her parents separated when she was only a few weeks old, and Byron left England soon afterwards. He died in Greece when Ada was eight.

Her mother, Lady Byron, was a well-educated woman who loved mathematics. She was worried that her daughter might become as wild and emotional as her father, so she gave Ada a strict education in science and numbers. Ada had private teachers from an early age. Even so, she had a strong imagination. As a young girl, she studied birds and tried to design a flying machine. She wrote about wings, materials and even steam power, and she called her project "flyology".

In 1833, when she was seventeen, Ada was introduced to Charles Babbage, a mathematician and inventor. At a party in his house, Babbage showed his guests a part of his "Difference Engine", a large calculating machine made of metal wheels. Most visitors saw only a clever toy. Ada, however, understood how it worked and why it was important. The two became friends and wrote to each other for many years.

Babbage soon had a more ambitious idea. He designed the Analytical Engine, a machine that could follow a series of instructions given on punched cards, an idea borrowed from weaving machines that made patterns in cloth. In many ways, it had the main parts of a modern computer, including a memory and a unit that did the calculations. Unfortunately, it was never built, mainly because of the cost and the difficulty of making such precise parts at that time.

In 1842 an Italian engineer published an article in French about the Analytical Engine. Ada translated it into English. Babbage suggested that she add some notes of her own. Her notes ended up about three times longer than the original article. In the last one, called Note G, she described step by step how the machine could calculate a complicated series of numbers known as Bernoulli numbers. Many people consider this the first published computer program.

Even more remarkable was her vision. Babbage mainly thought of his engine as a powerful calculator. Ada imagined much more. She suggested that if music or other symbols could be expressed as numbers, the machine might work with them as well. It might, for example, compose pieces of music. At the same time, she warned that the machine could not truly create anything new; it could only do what people told it to do. Computer scientists still discuss this idea today.

Ada's life was short. She suffered from poor health and died of cancer in 1852, at the age of thirty-six. For about a hundred years, her work was almost forgotten. When modern computers appeared, researchers rediscovered her notes. In 1980, a programming language was named Ada in her honour, and every October people celebrate Ada Lovelace Day to remember the achievements of women in science.

questions.q: Why did Ada's mother give her a strict education in mathematics?
options: She wanted Ada to work for Babbage.
She did not want Ada to become wild and emotional like her father.
Ada's school asked her to.
She wanted Ada to become a poet.
questions.explain: Metne göre Lady Byron, kızının babası gibi aşırı duygusal ve başına buyruk olmasından korktu; bu yüzden ona sıkı bir bilim ve matematik eğitimi verdi. Doğru cevap "She did not want Ada to become wild and emotional like her father."

questions.q: How was Ada's idea of the machine different from Babbage's?
options: She thought it was only a toy.
She wanted to build it from wood.
She believed it would never work.
She imagined it working with music and symbols, not only numbers.
questions.explain: Babbage makineyi daha çok güçlü bir hesap aracı olarak görürken Ada, müzik ve semboller sayılarla ifade edilirse makinenin onlarla da çalışabileceğini düşündü. Doğru cevap "She imagined it working with music and symbols, not only numbers."

title: Forty Years on the Road
text:
According to his own story, everything began with a dream. One night in 1630, a young man in Istanbul dreamed that he was in a mosque full of light. In the dream he met the Prophet Muhammad. He was so excited that, instead of asking for "şefaat", which means help on the day of judgement, he made a mistake and asked for "seyahat", which means travel. The Prophet smiled and gave him what he had asked for. The young man was Evliya Çelebi, and he spent most of the next forty years on the road.

Evliya was born in Istanbul in 1611. His father was the chief goldsmith of the palace, so the family was comfortable and well connected. Evliya received a good education. He learned to read the Quran beautifully, studied music and calligraphy, and spoke several languages. As a young man he even entertained the sultan, Murad IV, with his songs and funny stories.

But palace life was not enough for him. He started by exploring every street, mosque and market in Istanbul, writing down everything he saw. Then he began to travel further. Usually he joined the staff of officials or military commanders, which gave him safety and a reason to move from place to place. Over the years he visited almost every part of the Ottoman Empire and many places beyond it: the Caucasus, Persia, the Balkans, Crete, Egypt and Sudan. In 1665 he went with an Ottoman group to Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg Empire.

The result of these journeys is the Seyahatname, or "Book of Travels", a huge work in ten volumes. It is one of the longest travel books ever written. Evliya describes cities, castles, bridges and markets. He counts houses, shops and mosques, records the words of local languages and writes about food, clothes and customs. For historians today, it is an extraordinary source of information about everyday life in the seventeenth century.

However, readers must be careful. Evliya loved a good story, and he did not always separate facts from imagination. His numbers are often far too large. Some of his adventures seem impossible, and he occasionally describes places that he probably never visited. Yet these exaggerations are part of his charm. He writes with humour, curiosity and great affection for the people he met, and he clearly enjoyed surprising his readers.

Evliya never married and seems to have had no children. His travels were his life's work. He spent his last years in Cairo, where he continued writing until his death, probably around 1682. For a long time, the Seyahatname was little known outside a small group of scholars, and it was not fully published until the twentieth century.

Today he is celebrated far beyond Turkey. In 2011, the four hundredth anniversary of his birth, UNESCO included him in its list of important anniversaries. Walking and riding routes in Greece and Turkey now follow parts of his journeys, so modern travellers can see the same landscapes he described almost four centuries ago.

questions.q: What mistake did Evliya make in his dream?
options: He went to the wrong mosque.
He forgot the Prophet's name.
He asked for travel instead of help on the day of judgement.
He asked for gold instead of travel.
questions.explain: Rüyasında heyecandan "şefaat" yerine "seyahat" dedi ve kendisine seyahat verildi. Doğru cevap "He asked for travel instead of help on the day of judgement."

questions.q: Why must readers be careful with the Seyahatname?
options: Some numbers and stories are exaggerated or imagined.
It is written in a secret code.
Most of it was written by other people.
It describes only Istanbul.
questions.explain: Evliya iyi hikâyeyi severdi; sayıları çoğu zaman fazla büyüktür ve bazı maceralar imkânsız görünür. Doğru cevap "Some numbers and stories are exaggerated or imagined."

title: Four Days of Fire
text:
Shortly after midnight on Sunday, 2 September 1666, a fire started in a bakery in Pudding Lane, a narrow street near London Bridge. The baker, Thomas Farriner, made bread for the king's navy. His family woke up to find the ground floor full of smoke. They escaped through a window and over the roofs, but their maid was too frightened to climb out and became one of the first victims.

At first, nobody was very worried. Fires were common in London, and most of them were put out quickly. When the Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bludworth, was woken up and taken to see the flames, he was not impressed. According to the famous story, he said the fire was so small that a woman could put it out, and he went back to bed.

That was a serious mistake. The summer had been long and dry, and the city was built mostly of wood. The houses stood very close together, and their upper floors often hung over the narrow streets, almost touching the houses on the other side. Near the river there were warehouses full of oil, coal, wood and other materials that burned easily. Worst of all, a strong wind was blowing from the east, and it carried the flames from one roof to the next.

By Sunday morning the fire had reached the river. People threw their belongings into boats or carried them through the streets on their backs. One man who watched all this was Samuel Pepys, a government official who kept a detailed diary. He wrote about pigeons that did not want to leave their homes and fell with burnt wings. He also described how he buried his wine and his expensive Parmesan cheese in his garden to keep them safe.

The usual method of fighting large fires was to pull down houses in the path of the flames, so the fire had nothing more to burn. However, the Lord Mayor hesitated, because the owners would demand money for their lost houses. By the time the king, Charles II, ordered the houses to be destroyed, the fire was far too big. Later, gunpowder was used to blow up whole rows of buildings.

On Tuesday the fire reached St Paul's Cathedral, the great church at the centre of the city. Its roof was covered with lead, which melted and ran down the streets like a river. Finally, on Wednesday the wind dropped, and the firebreaks began to work.

The results were shocking. About 13,000 houses, almost ninety churches and many public buildings had been destroyed. Tens of thousands of people had lost their homes and camped in the fields outside the city. Officially, only a handful of deaths were recorded, but many historians believe the real number was much higher, because the deaths of poor people were often not counted.

London was rebuilt, this time mainly with brick and stone. The architect Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's Cathedral and dozens of other churches. Near Pudding Lane, a tall stone column called the Monument was built. It is about sixty-one metres high, the same as its distance from the bakery where the fire began.

questions.q: Which of these did NOT help the fire to spread?
options: A long, dry summer
Wooden houses standing close together
Brick and stone buildings
A strong wind from the east
questions.explain: Uzun kuru yaz, birbirine yakın ahşap evler ve doğudan esen güçlü rüzgâr yangını yaydı. Tuğla ve taş binalar ise ancak yangından sonra yaygınlaştı. Doğru cevap "Brick and stone buildings".

questions.q: What is special about the height of the Monument?
options: It is as tall as St Paul's Cathedral.
It has one step for every house that burned.
It was built from the stones of Pudding Lane.
Its height is the same as its distance from the bakery.
questions.explain: Anıt yaklaşık altmış bir metre yüksekliğindedir; bu, yangının başladığı fırına olan uzaklığıyla aynıdır. Doğru cevap "Its height is the same as its distance from the bakery."

title: Trapped in the Ice
text:
In August 1914, just as the First World War was beginning, a wooden ship called the Endurance left England for Antarctica. Its leader was the Irish-born explorer Ernest Shackleton. His plan was bold: he wanted his team to become the first people to cross the whole Antarctic continent on foot, from one coast to the other, passing through the South Pole.

The team never even reached the land. In January 1915, in the Weddell Sea, the ship became trapped in thick pack ice. The crew tried to cut a path with tools and saws, but it was hopeless. The ice closed around the Endurance and carried it slowly north with the currents. For months, the twenty-eight men lived on the frozen ship. They played football on the ice, trained the dogs and held concerts in the evenings to keep their spirits up.

The pressure of the moving ice was enormous, and slowly it began to crush the ship. In October the men had to leave it and set up camp on the ice. In November 1915, they watched the Endurance finally sink. They were now alone on a moving sheet of ice, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest human being, with no radio and no way to ask for help.

Shackleton knew that hope was as important as food. He stayed calm and cheerful in front of his men, gave his own warm gloves to others and kept everyone busy. For months they waited, eating seals and penguins, while the ice drifted north. In April 1916, the ice began to break up, and the men climbed into the three small lifeboats they had saved from the ship. After a terrible week at sea, cold, wet and almost without sleep, they reached Elephant Island, a rocky and empty place. It was the first time they had stood on solid ground for nearly a year and a half.

Nobody would ever look for them there. So Shackleton made a daring decision. He chose five men and set out in the largest lifeboat, the James Caird, which was only about seven metres long. Their goal was South Georgia, an island with a whaling station, about 1,300 kilometres away across one of the stormiest oceans in the world. For around two weeks, they fought huge waves and freezing spray. Their navigator, Frank Worsley, could only check their position with the sun on a few occasions. Yet they found the island.

Unfortunately, they landed on the wrong side of it. The whaling station was on the other coast, beyond mountains and glaciers that nobody had ever crossed. Shackleton, Worsley and Tom Crean walked for about thirty-six hours without stopping, with screws in their boots to grip the ice. When they finally walked into the station, the workers hardly recognised them.

Rescuing the men on Elephant Island took several attempts, because the sea ice blocked the way. At last, on 30 August 1916, a small Chilean ship reached the island. Shackleton counted the figures on the beach and saw that all of them were alive. Not a single member of the Endurance crew had died.

In 2022, almost a century later, an expedition found the wreck of the Endurance about three kilometres below the surface of the Weddell Sea. Its name could still be read clearly on the back of the ship.

questions.q: What was the original goal of Shackleton's expedition?
options: To find the wreck of an older ship
To cross the whole Antarctic continent on foot
To build a whaling station on South Georgia
To be the first to reach the South Pole
questions.explain: Shackleton'ın planı, Antarktika kıtasını Güney Kutbu'ndan geçerek bir kıyıdan diğerine yürüyerek geçmekti. Doğru cevap "To cross the whole Antarctic continent on foot".

questions.q: Why did Shackleton sail to South Georgia in a small lifeboat?
options: Nobody would come to look for them on Elephant Island.
He wanted to go home before the others.
The Endurance was waiting for him there.
The men on Elephant Island had already been rescued.
questions.explain: Elephant Island'da kimse onları aramayacaktı; bu yüzden Shackleton yardım bulmak için küçük filikayla balina istasyonunun bulunduğu South Georgia'ya yola çıktı. Doğru cevap "Nobody would come to look for them on Elephant Island."

title: Sunrise Among the Stone Heads
text:
The minibus left our hotel in Kahta at three o'clock in the morning. Outside, it was completely dark, and most of the passengers were still half asleep, wrapped in jackets and blankets. Our destination was the top of Mount Nemrut, a mountain more than two thousand metres high in the province of Adıyaman, and we wanted to be there before the sun came up.

The road climbed slowly through small villages and bare hills. After about two hours, the minibus stopped in a car park, and the driver told us to take our torches. The last part of the journey had to be done on foot: a steep path of loose stones that took around twenty minutes. The air was thin and cold, and even in July, I was glad I had brought a hat and gloves. All around me, I could hear people breathing hard and laughing nervously in the darkness.

At the top, there is something that surprises almost every visitor: a huge, artificial hill made of small broken stones, about fifty metres high. Archaeologists believe it covers the tomb of King Antiochus I, who ruled a small kingdom called Commagene in the first century BC. The kingdom was located between the powerful empires of Rome and Persia, and Antiochus seems to have wanted to show that his family was connected to both. Nobody has yet found the burial chamber itself, perhaps because digging into the loose stones is extremely difficult and dangerous.

On the east and west sides of the hill, there are terraces with giant stone statues of the king, gods and animals such as lions and eagles. The bodies of the statues are still sitting in long lines, but over the centuries, earthquakes and weather have knocked off their heads. Today the heads, each one about two metres tall, stand on the ground in front of them, as if someone had placed them there carefully. In 1987, the site was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List.

We went to the east terrace and found a place to sit among dozens of other people. Little by little, the sky changed from black to dark blue, and then a thin red line appeared over the mountains. When the first rays of the sun finally touched the stone faces, the crowd went silent. The heads, which had looked grey and cold a few minutes earlier, suddenly became warm and golden. It almost seemed as if their calm, serious eyes were opening after a long sleep.

I sat there for a long time, thinking about the king who had wanted to be remembered forever. In a way, he had succeeded, since people still climb his mountain in the dark more than two thousand years later. But his kingdom had disappeared, and his own face lay on the ground, looking out over the land he once ruled. On the way back down, nobody in the minibus slept.

questions.q: Why are the heads of the statues on the ground?
options: Visitors moved them for photographs
The king ordered them to be placed there
Earthquakes and weather knocked them off over the centuries
They were never attached to the bodies
questions.explain: Metne göre yüzyıllar boyunca depremler ve hava koşulları heykellerin başlarını düşürdü; doğru cevap "Earthquakes and weather knocked them off over the centuries".

questions.q: What do archaeologists believe the artificial hill covers?
options: A Roman city
The tomb of King Antiochus I
A secret road to Persia
An old village
questions.explain: Arkeologlar yapay tepenin Kral I. Antiochos’un mezarını örttüğüne inanıyor; doğru cevap "The tomb of King Antiochus I".

title: A Week at the Edinburgh Fringe
text:
Every August, the population of Edinburgh seems to double. Actors, comedians, musicians, dancers and hundreds of thousands of visitors arrive in the Scottish capital for a group of festivals, and the biggest and wildest of them is the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. Last summer, my friend Ece, who studies theatre, persuaded me to spend a week there with her.

The story of the Fringe began in 1947, when the first Edinburgh International Festival was organised after the Second World War. Eight theatre groups who had not been invited decided to come anyway and perform on the edges, or the "fringe", of the official programme. The idea became a tradition. Today the Fringe has a simple and unusual rule: anyone can take part. There is no committee that chooses the shows, so if you can find a place to perform and pay to register, you are in. As a result, the programme lists thousands of different shows every year.

Our first morning taught us how serious this is. On the Royal Mile, the long, sloping street that runs through the old town from the castle, there were performers everywhere. A man was juggling knives while standing on a ladder. A group of students in white make-up were performing a silent play. Every few metres, someone pushed a flyer into our hands and asked us to come to their show. By lunchtime, my bag was full of colourful pieces of paper.

The shows happen in every possible space: proper theatres, but also university lecture rooms, church halls, cafés, tiny rooms above bars, and even a large purple tent shaped like an upside-down cow. Some performances are famous and sold out for weeks. Others are free, and the performers simply ask the audience to put a little money in a bucket at the end, if they enjoyed it.

We decided on a strategy. Every day, we would see one show that had good reviews and one show we knew nothing about. The results were mixed but always interesting. We saw a brilliant comedy about a Scottish grandmother who becomes a spy, an emotional dance piece about refugees, and a strange one-man show in which the actor spoke only in questions. Once we were the only two people in the audience, and the young performer did the whole hour for us anyway, with enormous energy.

Of course, there are less romantic sides as well. Hotels and rooms become extremely expensive in August, and many performers lose money because the costs of travelling, staying and advertising are so high. Ece told me that for many young artists, it is still worth it, because one good review or one important person in the audience can change a career.

On our last night, we climbed Calton Hill and watched the lights of the city below us. I had seen fourteen shows in seven days, and I could not decide which one was my favourite. Ece just smiled and said, "Next year, we bring our own show."

questions.q: How did the Fringe begin?
options: A university started a theatre competition
Eight groups who were not invited came and performed anyway
The government asked artists to entertain soldiers
A famous comedian organised the first show
questions.explain: 1947’de davet edilmeyen sekiz tiyatro grubu yine de gelip resmî programın kenarında sahne aldı; doğru cevap "Eight groups who were not invited came and performed anyway".

questions.q: Why is it still worth going for many young artists, according to Ece?
options: Because the hotels are cheap in August
Because every performer receives money from the city
Because the shows are always sold out
Because one good review or an important person can change a career
questions.explain: Ece’ye göre tek bir iyi eleştiri ya da salondaki önemli bir kişi bir kariyeri değiştirebilir; doğru cevap "Because one good review or an important person can change a career".

title: Islands of Stone in Ha Long Bay
text:
We left Hanoi early in the morning, and after a bus journey of around three hours, we arrived at the busy harbour where dozens of wooden boats were waiting. Our boat was a traditional-looking ship with dark red sails, although, as the captain admitted with a smile, the sails were mostly for decoration and the engine did the real work. For the next two days, it would be our home in Ha Long Bay, one of the most famous landscapes in Vietnam.

Within half an hour of leaving the harbour, the view became almost unreal. All around us, tall islands of grey and green rock rose straight out of the calm, emerald water. Some were as big as hills, covered with thick forest; others were just thin towers of stone, hardly wider than a house. There are roughly sixteen hundred of these islands and islets in the bay, and most of them have no people living on them, because their steep sides make it almost impossible to build anything.

The islands are made of limestone, a type of rock that slowly dissolves in rainwater. Over millions of years, rain, wind and the sea have cut the rock into these strange shapes and created many caves inside them. Local legend offers a more poetic explanation. According to the story, a family of dragons came down from the sky to protect the land from invaders and dropped jewels into the sea, which turned into the islands. In fact, the name Ha Long is often translated as "descending dragon".

In the afternoon, we visited one of the largest caves, which is reached by a long stairway from the water. Inside, there were huge rooms with high ceilings and rock formations that hung down like icicles. Our guide, Linh, pointed out shapes that local people say look like animals and gods, although I needed a lot of imagination to see most of them.

Later, we paddled kayaks through a low natural tunnel into a hidden lagoon, completely surrounded by cliffs. It was so quiet that we could hear monkeys moving in the trees above us. Linh explained that the bay has long been home to fishing communities, some of whom lived in floating villages built on rafts. In recent years, many families have moved to land, partly because of the growth of tourism and efforts to protect the water.

Tourism has brought money and jobs to the region, but it has also created problems, such as rubbish in the water and heavy boat traffic. Linh told us that rules have become stricter and that many boats now try to reduce plastic. On our boat, we drank from glass bottles and refilled them from a large water tank.

That night, I sat on the deck while the other passengers slept. The islands were dark shapes against a sky full of stars, and the water was perfectly still. I thought about the dragons in the story and decided that, scientific or not, it was a good explanation.

questions.q: Why do most of the islands have no people living on them?
options: Because dragons live there
Because their steep sides make building almost impossible
Because the government does not allow visitors
Because they are covered by water at night
questions.explain: Adaların dik yamaçları üzerlerine bir şey inşa etmeyi neredeyse imkânsız kılıyor; doğru cevap "Because their steep sides make building almost impossible".

questions.q: What is one problem that tourism has created in the bay?
options: Rubbish in the water and heavy boat traffic
A lack of jobs
Too many monkeys on the islands
The disappearance of the caves
questions.explain: Metne göre turizm suya karışan çöp ve yoğun tekne trafiği gibi sorunlar doğurdu; doğru cevap "Rubbish in the water and heavy boat traffic".

title: Clouds over Machu Picchu
text:
I had seen so many photographs of Machu Picchu before my trip to Peru that I was almost afraid of being disappointed. Could any real place be as perfect as those pictures? As it turned out, my first view of the ancient city was nothing like the photographs at all, because it was completely hidden by cloud.

My journey had started a few days earlier in Cusco, the old capital of the Inca Empire, which lies at about 3,400 metres above sea level. Like many visitors, I spent my first two days there feeling tired and short of breath, because the body needs time to adjust to such heights. Local people recommended drinking coca tea, walking slowly and avoiding heavy meals, and I followed their advice carefully.

There are two main ways to reach Machu Picchu. The more adventurous one is the Inca Trail, a walk of about four days along ancient stone paths over high mountain passes. The number of hikers is limited each day, so permits often sell out months in advance. I had left it too late, so I chose the second option: a scenic train ride through the valley of the Urubamba River to the small town of Aguas Calientes, followed by a short bus ride up a road full of tight bends.

Machu Picchu was probably built in the fifteenth century, perhaps as a royal estate for an Inca emperor. Its builders were extraordinary engineers. The stones in the most important walls were cut so precisely that they fit together without any mortar, and many of them have survived centuries of earthquakes. Farming terraces climb the steep slopes like giant stairs, and a clever system of channels carried water through the site. Local farmers knew about the ruins, but the site became famous around the world after the American explorer Hiram Bingham visited it in 1911 and wrote about it.

When I walked through the entrance at seven in the morning, all I could see was white mist. I could make out a few walls near me, and a llama calmly eating grass beside the path, but nothing more. Other visitors around me looked as disappointed as I felt. A guide nearby told his group to be patient. "The mountain decides when to show itself," he said.

He was right. About half an hour later, the clouds began to move. First the tops of the mountains appeared, sharp and green, then the terraces, and finally the whole city, spread out on its narrow ridge between deep valleys. People around me started clapping. For a few minutes, the view was exactly like the photographs, and yet it felt completely different, because I was standing inside it.

Today the number of daily visitors is limited, and visitors must follow fixed routes, partly to protect the old stones from damage. I think this is a good thing. Machu Picchu has survived for more than five hundred years, and it deserves to survive for many more.

questions.q: Why did the writer not walk the Inca Trail?
options: Because it was closed for repairs
Because the writer felt too ill
Because the writer had left it too late to get a permit
Because it was more expensive than the train
questions.explain: Patikada günlük yürüyüşçü sayısı sınırlı ve izinler aylar önce tükeniyor; yazar geç kalmıştı, doğru cevap "Because the writer had left it too late to get a permit".

questions.q: What did the guide mean when he said "The mountain decides when to show itself"?
options: Visitors must wait for the clouds to move
Visitors must climb to the top of the mountain
The site closes when it rains
Only guides can see the whole city
questions.explain: Rehber bulutların açılmasını beklemek gerektiğini, sabırlı olmalarını söylüyor; doğru cevap "Visitors must wait for the clouds to move".

title: A Boat to Akdamar Island
text:
The first thing that surprised me about Lake Van was its colour. I had expected an ordinary lake, but the water was an intense turquoise blue, almost like a tropical sea, and it stretched so far that I could not see the other side. It is the largest lake in Türkiye, and it sits at about 1,650 metres above sea level, surrounded by mountains that were still covered with snow in early June.

My friend Baran, who grew up in Van, had promised to show me his favourite place: Akdamar Island, a small rocky island near the southern shore. We drove from the city for about forty minutes and then waited at a little pier in Gevaş for a boat. While we waited, Baran asked me to put my hand in the water and then rub my fingers together. They felt strangely slippery, almost like soap. He explained that Lake Van is a soda lake; its water is both salty and very alkaline, so most kinds of fish cannot survive in it.

There is one remarkable exception, a small silver fish called the pearl mullet, or inci kefali. It has adapted to the difficult conditions of the lake. Every spring, millions of these fish swim up the freshwater rivers that flow into the lake to lay their eggs, jumping over small waterfalls along the way. Baran said that watching them is one of the great sights of the region, and that fishing is restricted during this season to protect them.

The boat trip to the island took about twenty minutes. As we came closer, I saw a church of reddish-brown stone standing on a slope among almond trees. This is the Church of the Holy Cross, which was built in the early tenth century for an Armenian king named Gagik I, whose palace was once on the island. Today the palace has disappeared, but the church has survived for more than a thousand years.

What makes the church so special is its outside walls. They are covered with carvings: scenes from Bible stories, such as Jonah and the whale and David and Goliath, along with images of animals, plants and the king himself holding a model of the church. Some of the figures are surprisingly lively, and Baran and I spent a long time trying to identify them. After many years of neglect, the building was carefully restored and reopened as a museum in 2007, and since then it has attracted visitors from Türkiye and abroad.

We climbed the hill behind the church and sat on a rock looking out over the lake. In the distance, the snowy peak of Mount Süphan was reflected in the still water. Baran opened a bag and brought out cheese, bread and fresh herbs that his mother had prepared for us.

"Now you understand why I always come back," he said. I did. On our way back to the city, we stopped at a centre that cares for the famous Van cats, white cats that often have one blue eye and one amber eye. It was a fitting end to a day full of unexpected colours.

questions.q: Why can most kinds of fish not live in Lake Van?
options: Because the water is too cold
Because the water is salty and very alkaline
Because the lake is too deep
Because there are too many boats
questions.explain: Van Gölü bir soda gölü; suyu hem tuzlu hem de çok alkali olduğu için çoğu balık yaşayamıyor; doğru cevap "Because the water is salty and very alkaline".

questions.q: What makes the Church of the Holy Cross special, according to the text?
options: Its golden roof
Its very tall tower
The paintings inside the palace
The carvings on its outside walls
questions.explain: Metne göre kiliseyi özel kılan, dış duvarlarındaki oymalardır; doğru cevap "The carvings on its outside walls".

title: The Mysterious Rays of Würzburg
text:
On a cold evening in November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was working alone in his laboratory at the University of Würzburg.
