Like many scientists of his time, he was experimenting with glass tubes from which most of the air had been removed. When a strong electric current passed through such a tube, it produced a strange glow. To study the effect more carefully, Röntgen had covered the tube completely with thick black cardboard, so that no light could escape.

Then he noticed something that should not have been possible. Across the dark room, a small screen painted with a special chemical was glowing faintly. The tube was covered, so ordinary light could not be reaching it. Something invisible was coming out of the tube, passing through the cardboard and travelling through the air.

Röntgen was a careful and private man, and he did not tell anyone at first. For several weeks, he worked almost without stopping, testing his discovery. According to some accounts, he even ate and slept in the laboratory. He placed different objects between the tube and the screen: paper, wood, a thick book. The rays went through almost all of them. Metal, however, blocked them. Then, while holding a small piece of lead in front of the screen, he saw something astonishing: the faint shadow of the bones inside his own hand.

Because he did not know what these rays were, he called them "X-rays," using the letter that mathematicians use for an unknown value. In late December, he asked his wife, Anna Bertha, to place her hand on a photographic plate. The image that appeared showed her bones and her wedding ring clearly. She is often reported to have said, "I have seen my death." The picture became one of the most famous images in the history of science.

When Röntgen published his findings at the end of 1895, the news spread around the world with remarkable speed. Within weeks, scientists everywhere were building their own machines, and within months, doctors were using X-rays to find broken bones and bullets inside patients' bodies. In 1901, Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. Interestingly, he refused to take out a patent, because he believed his discovery should benefit everyone.

There was, however, a darker side. At first, nobody understood that X-rays could damage living tissue. Early researchers and doctors often worked with them every day without protection, and many developed serious burns and illnesses. It took years before people learned to use protective shields and to limit the amount of exposure.

Today, X-rays are used in hospitals, at airports and even to study the structure of molecules. All of this began with a faint glow in a dark room and a scientist who refused to ignore it.

questions.q: What first made Röntgen realise that something unusual was happening?
options: A screen across the room glowed although the tube was covered
His wife complained about a strange light
The cardboard around the tube caught fire
He saw a broken bone in a patient
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "A screen across the room glowed although the tube was covered": tüp siyah kartonla tamamen kaplı olmasına rağmen odanın öbür ucundaki ekran hafifçe parlıyordu.

questions.q: Why did Röntgen not take out a patent on X-rays?
options: He did not have enough money
He thought the discovery should benefit everyone
Another scientist had already done it
He believed the rays were too dangerous
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "He thought the discovery should benefit everyone": metne göre buluşunun herkese fayda sağlaması gerektiğine inandığı için patent almayı reddetti.

title: The Face the Moon Always Shows Us
text:
If you look at the full Moon tonight, you will see the same dark and light shapes that your grandparents saw, and that people saw thousands of years ago. Some cultures imagined a face in those shapes, others a rabbit or a woman carrying wood. But they all saw the same pattern. That is because the Moon always shows the same side to the Earth. For most of human history, nobody had any idea what the other side looked like.

At first, this might suggest that the Moon does not spin at all. In fact, it does spin, but very slowly. It turns once on its axis in roughly the same time that it takes to travel once around the Earth, about twenty-seven days. Because these two movements are perfectly matched, the same face is always turned towards us. Astronomers call this tidal locking.

How did such a perfect match happen? The answer lies in gravity. Billions of years ago, the young Moon was closer to the Earth and probably spun much faster. The Earth's gravity pulled on it so strongly that it stretched the Moon very slightly, creating a small bulge on each side. As the Moon turned, the Earth kept pulling on these bulges, acting a little like a brake. Over a very long time, this slowed the Moon's spin until it matched its orbit. Many other moons in our solar system have become locked to their planets in the same way.

People sometimes call the hidden half "the dark side of the Moon," but this is misleading. The far side receives just as much sunlight as the near side. When we see a new Moon from Earth, the far side is actually in full daylight. It is only "dark" in the sense that it was unknown to us.

That changed in 1959, when the Soviet spacecraft Luna 3 flew around the Moon and sent back the first blurry photographs of the far side. Scientists were surprised. The far side looked quite different, with far fewer of the large dark plains that make up the "face" we know, and many more craters. Experts are still discussing the reasons for this difference. Much later, in 2019, the Chinese mission Chang'e 4 became the first to land gently on the far side.

The relationship between the Earth and the Moon is still changing today. Thanks to mirrors left on the surface by Apollo astronauts, scientists can fire lasers at the Moon and measure its distance very precisely. They have found that it is moving away from us by about four centimetres every year. At the same time, the Moon's pull is slowly making the Earth's days longer, although the change is far too small for anyone to notice in a lifetime.

So the familiar face in the night sky is the result of a very long dance, one that is not finished yet.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
options: The Moon does not spin at all
The far side is always dark
The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around the Earth
Clouds on the Moon hide the other side
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around the Earth": Ay kendi ekseni etrafında, Dünya'nın çevresinde bir tur attığı sürede (yaklaşık 27 gün) bir kez döner.

questions.q: Why is the expression "the dark side of the Moon" misleading?
options: The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side
The far side is covered in ice
Astronauts live on the far side
The far side is closer to the Sun
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side": uzak yüz de yakın yüz kadar güneş ışığı alır; yalnızca bizim için bilinmez olduğu anlamında "karanlıktır".

title: Try Not to Yawn
text:
Here is a small experiment. While you read this text, notice whether you feel the urge to yawn. Many people do, simply because they are reading or thinking about yawning. If you are in a room with other people, you might even see someone yawn and then feel your own mouth begin to open. Yawning, it seems, is contagious. But why should something so ordinary spread from person to person?

First, it is worth asking why we yawn at all. Surprisingly, scientists still do not fully agree. For a long time, people believed that we yawn because our blood needs more oxygen. However, experiments in the 1980s found that breathing air with extra oxygen did not make people yawn less, and breathing air with more carbon dioxide did not make them yawn more. That popular explanation therefore seems unlikely.

A newer idea, supported by the psychologist Andrew Gallup and others, is that yawning helps to cool the brain. A deep yawn stretches the jaw, increases blood flow and brings in a large amount of air. Some studies have found that people yawn less when they hold a cold pack to their forehead, and that yawning changes with the temperature of the air outside. According to this theory, a yawn may help the brain to stay alert, which could explain why we often yawn when we are bored or about to change activity. This explanation is promising, but it has not been proved.

Contagious yawning is an even more curious puzzle. Researchers have noticed that it does not appear immediately in life. Babies yawn, and even unborn babies have been seen yawning in scans, but young children rarely catch yawns from others. The ability usually seems to develop around the age of four or five. Some studies suggest that people are more likely to catch a yawn from family members and close friends than from strangers.

Because of these patterns, some scientists have linked contagious yawning to empathy, our ability to understand and share other people's feelings. The idea is that we unconsciously copy the people we feel connected to. However, this link is still debated, and several large studies have found only weak evidence for it.

Humans are not the only species that do this. Chimpanzees seem to catch yawns from each other, especially from members of their own group. Some experiments have even suggested that dogs may yawn after hearing or seeing their owners yawn, although the results have been mixed.

So, did you yawn while reading this? If you did, do not worry. It is not a sign that the text was boring. It may simply be a sign that your brain is social, and perhaps that it was getting a little warm.

questions.q: What happened when people breathed air with extra oxygen?
options: They stopped yawning completely
They yawned much more
They became very sleepy
They did not yawn less
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "They did not yawn less": 1980'lerdeki deneylerde fazladan oksijen solumak esnemeyi azaltmadı; bu yüzden "oksijen ihtiyacı" açıklaması pek olası görünmüyor.

questions.q: At about what age does contagious yawning usually begin?
options: Before birth
Around four or five years old
Around twelve years old
Only in adulthood
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Around four or five years old": bebekler esner, ama başkasından esneme kapma yeteneği genellikle dört beş yaş civarında gelişir.

title: A Lamp Swinging in Pisa
text:
According to a story that has been told for centuries, a young medical student named Galileo Galilei was sitting in the cathedral of Pisa one day in the early 1580s. Instead of listening to the service, he was watching a large lamp hanging from the ceiling. A draught of air had set it swinging. Sometimes the swings were wide, and sometimes, as the movement slowed down, they were much smaller.

Galileo noticed something strange. Even when the swings became smaller, each one seemed to take the same amount of time. There were no watches with second hands in those days, so he measured the time using his own pulse. The result appeared to be the same: a long swing and a short swing lasted about equally long.

Historians are not sure whether this famous scene really happened exactly like this. The story comes mainly from Galileo's student and first biographer, Vincenzo Viviani, who wrote it down many years later and may have made it more dramatic. However, we know that Galileo did study pendulums seriously. In his later experiments, he hung weights on strings of different lengths and timed their movements. He found that the time of each swing depends mainly on the length of the string, not on the weight or on how wide the swing is, at least when the swings are fairly small.

This may sound like a small detail, but it was extremely important. If a pendulum always swings at a regular rate, it can be used to measure time. In Galileo's day, the best mechanical clocks could easily be wrong by a quarter of an hour in a single day. Near the end of his life, when he was old and almost blind, Galileo designed a clock controlled by a pendulum. He died in 1642, before it could be built.

The Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens achieved what Galileo had imagined. In 1656, he built the first working pendulum clock. Its accuracy was a dramatic improvement: instead of losing or gaining many minutes a day, it was wrong by perhaps less than a minute, and later versions became even better. For nearly three hundred years, pendulum clocks were the most accurate timekeepers in the world, and the tall "grandfather clocks" in old houses are their direct descendants.

Pendulums also helped to answer bigger questions. In 1851, the French physicist Léon Foucault hung a heavy ball on a very long wire in Paris. As the hours passed, the direction of its swing slowly turned. This was clear, visible evidence that the Earth itself was rotating underneath it.

Whether or not Galileo really timed a lamp with his pulse, the story carries an important lesson. Great discoveries often begin when someone looks carefully at something that everyone else has seen a thousand times.

questions.q: What did Galileo discover about the time of each swing?
options: It depends mainly on the weight at the end
It is always exactly one second
It depends mainly on the length of the string
It changes with the temperature of the room
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "It depends mainly on the length of the string": deneylerinde salınım süresinin ağırlığa ya da salınımın genişliğine değil, esas olarak ipin uzunluğuna bağlı olduğunu buldu.

questions.q: What did Foucault's pendulum show?
options: That the Earth rotates
That clocks were not accurate
That Galileo's story was false
That heavy balls swing faster
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "That the Earth rotates": Paris'teki sarkacın salınım yönünün saatler içinde yavaşça dönmesi, Dünya'nın kendi etrafında döndüğünün görünür bir kanıtıydı.

title: The Smiling Creature That Regrows Its Body
text:
With its wide, smiling mouth, small eyes and feathery pink gills sticking out from its head like a crown, the axolotl looks more like a cartoon character than a real animal. Yet this small amphibian, which is a type of salamander, is one of the most studied creatures in modern biology. Scientists around the world keep it in their laboratories because of an extraordinary ability: it can regrow large parts of its body.

The axolotl comes from just one place on Earth: the lakes and canals around Mexico City, especially the old waterways of Xochimilco. Its name comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, and it is often connected with Xolotl, a god who, according to legend, turned himself into an axolotl to escape death.

Unlike most salamanders, the axolotl never really grows up. Frogs and many other amphibians begin life in water and later change their bodies so that they can live on land. The axolotl usually stays in its young form for its whole life. It keeps its gills, lives permanently in water and can still have babies. Scientists call this unusual situation neoteny.

Its most famous talent, however, is regeneration. If an axolotl loses a leg, perhaps in a fight, it can grow a complete new one, with bones, muscles and nerves, in a matter of weeks. Remarkably, the new leg usually works perfectly and leaves no scar. It can also repair its tail, parts of its heart and spinal cord, and even some areas of its brain. Humans can heal a cut finger, but we cannot replace a lost hand. Researchers hope that by understanding which genes and cells allow the axolotl to rebuild itself, they might one day find ways to help people heal better after serious injuries. This goal is still far away, and nobody should expect quick miracles.

There is a sad irony in the axolotl's story. While millions of these animals live in laboratories and home aquariums around the world, they are critically endangered in the wild. Mexico City has grown enormously, many canals have been filled in or polluted, and fish introduced from other countries eat young axolotls. Surveys over the past few decades have found fewer and fewer of them, and in some recent searches, researchers struggled to find any at all.

Local people and scientists are now trying to help. Some farmers in Xochimilco use traditional methods, with clean water channels around their fields, to create safe places for the animals. The axolotl has also become a national symbol in Mexico and even appears on a banknote.

It would be a great loss if an animal that can regrow almost anything could not survive the changes humans have made to its only home.

questions.q: What is unusual about how an axolotl grows up?
options: It moves from water to land very early
It usually stays in its young form all its life
It grows much faster than other animals
It changes colour every year
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "It usually stays in its young form all its life": aksolotl çoğu semenderin aksine genç formunu korur, solungaçlarıyla hep suda yaşar; buna neoteni denir.

questions.q: Why are wild axolotls in danger?
options: Scientists take too many of them to laboratories
They cannot regrow their gills
Their home has been damaged by the growing city, pollution and foreign fish
They are hunted for banknotes
questions.explain: Doğru cevap "Their home has been damaged by the growing city, pollution and foreign fish": Mexico City büyüdükçe kanallar dolduruldu ya da kirlendi, dışarıdan getirilen balıklar da yavruları yiyor.

title: Notes in the Margins
text:
Ayla had worked at the public library in Samsun for six years, and she thought she had seen every kind of reader. There were the students who fell asleep on their books before exams, the retired men who argued quietly about newspapers and the children who wanted only books about dinosaurs. But in October, she discovered a reader she could not explain.

It began with a novel that had been returned through the book drop one rainy night. As Ayla checked it for damage, she noticed small handwritten notes in pencil along the edges of the pages. Writing in library books was strictly forbidden, and normally she would have been annoyed. These notes, however, were different. They were funny, kind and surprisingly clever. Next to a sad scene, someone had written, “Don’t worry, she comes back in chapter twelve.” Next to a long description of a garden, the note said, “I have never seen a garden like this, but I would like to.”

Over the following weeks, Ayla found the same handwriting in more books: a travel guide to Norway, a cookbook from Gaziantep, a book of poems and, strangely, a beginner’s guide to astronomy. In the astronomy book, there was a small drawing of the moon with a smiling face. Ayla began to look forward to the returns each morning, like someone waiting for letters.

She checked the records, but all the books had been borrowed using different cards, many of them belonging to members of the same family. That made the mystery even more confusing. Was it a whole family of secret writers, or one person using other people’s cards?

Ayla decided to leave a reply. In the next book with the mysterious handwriting, she placed a small piece of paper, not writing on the page itself, of course. “Dear reader,” she wrote. “Your notes have made my mornings better. But please use paper, not pencil. The library needs its books. Who are you?”

For two weeks, nothing happened. Then the book came back with a new piece of paper inside, written in the same careful hand. “I am sorry about the pencil,” it said. “I am eighty-one years old and I cannot walk to the library anymore. My grandchildren bring me books with their cards. I write in them because I have nobody to talk to about what I read.”

The note was signed simply, “Bedia, Atakum.”

Ayla read it three times. That evening, she talked to her manager, and together they made a plan. The library had a home delivery service for elderly readers, but few people knew about it. The following Saturday, Ayla herself carried a bag of books to a small flat near the sea in Atakum.

Bedia Hanım was tiny, with sharp eyes and a voice full of laughter. She apologised again for the pencil marks, and Ayla laughed and forgave her immediately. They spent the afternoon drinking coffee and arguing happily about the ending of the novel.

Now, on the first Saturday of every month, Ayla visits Bedia Hanım with new books. The pencil notes have stopped. Instead, the two women have started a small reading club in the community centre near Bedia Hanım’s home. It has eleven members, and every one of them is encouraged to say exactly what they think in the margins of the conversation.

questions.q: Why did the mysterious reader write notes in the books?
options: She wanted to annoy the librarians.
She was a teacher marking mistakes.
She had nobody to talk to about what she read.
Her grandchildren asked her to.
questions.explain: Bedia Hanım okuduklarını konuşacak kimsesi olmadığı için yazıyordu: "She had nobody to talk to about what she read."

questions.q: What changed after Ayla visited Bedia Hanım?
options: Bedia Hanım stopped reading.
They started a small reading club together.
The library stopped its delivery service.
Bedia Hanım moved to Samsun city centre.
questions.explain: İkisi birlikte küçük bir okuma kulübü kurdu: "They started a small reading club together."

title: A Wallet in Tokyo
text:
On his third day in Tokyo, Kaan realised that his wallet was gone. He was standing at the ticket machine in a busy station, surrounded by thousands of people moving quickly in every direction, and his back pocket was empty. Inside the wallet were his credit cards, his student card, about thirty thousand yen and a small photograph of his family that he had carried for years.

For a moment, he simply stood there, unable to think. He was a computer science student from Gaziantep on a short programme at a Japanese university, and he had heard many stories about how safe Japan was. But this was one of the largest cities in the world. How could anyone find one small wallet among so many people?

His Japanese classmate, Haruka, did not seem worried at all. “First, we go to the koban,” she said calmly. A koban, she explained, is a small neighbourhood police box, and you can find them all over Japanese cities. The officers inside give directions, help lost children and, very often, deal with lost property.

The koban near the station was tiny, with two polite officers and a desk covered in neat forms. Kaan described his wallet in detail while Haruka translated: brown leather, slightly old, with a scratch on one corner. One officer typed everything carefully into a computer and gave him a reference number. “If someone brings it, we will call you,” he said, bowing slightly.

Kaan thanked him, but he did not feel hopeful. That evening, he cancelled his credit cards and called his parents, trying to sound relaxed. His mother was more upset about the family photograph than about the money. It was the only copy of a picture taken at his grandfather’s last birthday.

The next two days were difficult. Haruka lent him some money, and he spent hours worrying about his student card. Then, on the third morning, his phone rang. It was the police. His wallet had been handed in at another station, nearly ten kilometres away, and he could collect it that afternoon.

When he opened the wallet at the police station, he could hardly believe his eyes. Everything was there: every card, every coin and every note, exactly thirty-one thousand two hundred yen. Behind the cards, the family photograph was still safe. The officer explained that a high school student had found it on a train seat and had taken it to the nearest police station on her way home from school.

Kaan asked if he could thank her. The officer checked, and the girl had agreed to share her contact information. Through Haruka, Kaan sent her a message and a small box of Turkish delight that his mother had posted to him. A few days later, a reply arrived, written in simple English with a little drawing of a train. “I think the wallet was a little lost,” it said. “I only helped it go home.”

Back in Gaziantep, Kaan often tells this story to his friends. Some of them doubt it at first. But he does not tell it to praise one country or criticise another. He tells it because, as he says, one honest teenager on a train taught him something no lecture ever did: small acts of honesty can travel much further than we imagine.

questions.q: What was Kaan's mother most worried about?
options: The money in the wallet.
The family photograph.
Kaan's student card.
The credit cards.
questions.explain: Annesi parayla değil, tek kopyası olan aile fotoğrafıyla ilgili üzülüyordu: "The family photograph."

questions.q: Who found Kaan's wallet?
options: One of the police officers.
Haruka's brother.
A taxi driver.
A high school student on a train.
questions.explain: Cüzdanı trende bir lise öğrencisi buldu ve karakola götürdü: "A high school student on a train."

title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
text:
My grandmother, Sabiha, grew up in a lighthouse. Whenever she told people this, they looked at her as if she had said she grew up on the moon. But for the first fifteen years of her life, home was a white stone tower on a rocky point of land, far from the nearest village, with the sea on three sides and a narrow dirt road on the fourth.

Her father was the lighthouse keeper. In those days, before automatic systems, someone had to climb the tower every evening, light the lamp and make sure it burned all night. Ships depended on that light to avoid the rocks below. My great-grandfather took the job extremely seriously. He polished the glass every morning, wrote careful notes about the weather and never, in twenty-two years, let the lamp go out.

My grandmother’s childhood was lonely in some ways, but she never described it as sad. She had no neighbours of her own age, so the sea became her friend. She knew the names of the winds and could predict a storm by the colour of the sky. She collected shells, learned to fish from the rocks and read every book that the supply boat brought once a month. Sometimes she spent whole afternoons watching dolphins far out in the water.

The story she told most often happened in the winter when she was twelve. Her father had fallen ill with a high fever, and her mother had gone to the village two days earlier to help a relative. The weather was getting worse by the hour. By evening, the wind was screaming around the tower, and heavy rain was hitting the windows.

My grandmother knew what to do, because she had watched her father hundreds of times. But knowing something and doing it alone are very different things. She climbed the long spiral staircase with a lantern in her hand, counting the steps to stay calm. At the top, her hands were shaking so much that it took her four attempts to light the lamp. Finally, the great light began to turn, sending its beam out over the dark, wild water.

She stayed up all night, checking the lamp, bringing water to her father and climbing the stairs again and again. Around midnight, through the rain, she saw the lights of a fishing boat moving slowly past the rocks. She would never know who was on it, but she was sure, until the end of her life, that the light had helped them get home.

In the morning, the storm had passed. Her father’s fever had dropped, and when he understood what had happened, he could not speak for a while. Then he took her up the tower, showed her the logbook and asked her to write the night’s notes herself, in her own handwriting.

Years later, my grandmother became a teacher and lived in a busy city. The lighthouse became automatic long ago, and nobody lives there now. But she kept a photograph of that page from the logbook on her wall. Beneath the weather notes, in a child’s careful letters, it says: “Wind very strong. Lamp burned all night. Keeper: Sabiha, age twelve.”

questions.q: Why did Sabiha have to light the lamp alone that night?
options: Her father was ill and her mother was away.
Her father had gone fishing.
The lamp had become automatic.
Her parents had asked her to practise.
questions.explain: Babası yüksek ateşle hastaydı ve annesi köydeydi: "Her father was ill and her mother was away."

questions.q: What did her father ask her to do the next morning?
options: Clean the glass of the lamp.
Go to the village to find her mother.
Leave the lighthouse and go to school.
Write the night's notes in the logbook herself.
questions.explain: Babası ondan gecenin notlarını kayıt defterine kendi el yazısıyla yazmasını istedi: "Write the night's notes in the logbook herself."

title: The Violin Next Door
text:
When Can moved into his new flat in Kadıköy, the estate agent had promised him that the building was “very quiet”. For the first week, this was true. Then, on Sunday morning at exactly eight o’clock, the violin began.

It came from the flat next door, through the thin wall of his bedroom. It was not beautiful music. It was the same short piece, played slowly, again and again, with frequent mistakes. Sometimes the player stopped in the middle of a note, as if annoyed, and began from the beginning. This continued for an hour, every single morning, including weekends.

Can worked late as a sound engineer, and he valued his sleep more than almost anything. After two weeks, he was exhausted and irritated. He wrote a polite but firm note, planning to leave it on his neighbour’s door. Then he changed his mind and decided it would be better to speak in person.

He knocked on the door, ready to complain. It was opened by a tall, elderly man in a cardigan, holding a violin in one hand. He had a kind, slightly embarrassed face. Before Can could say anything, the man spoke. “You must be the new neighbour. I am terribly sorry about the noise. I know it is awful.”

His name was Ruhi Bey, and he was seventy-eight years old. He invited Can in for tea, and although Can had planned a short conversation, he stayed for an hour. Ruhi Bey explained that he had been a mathematics teacher all his life. As a boy, he had dreamed of playing the violin, but his family had no money for lessons. Last year, after his wife died, his daughter had given him a violin as a present. “She said it was time,” he explained. “I am learning from videos on the internet. My teacher is a young man in Canada who has never heard of me.”

He was practising one particular piece, he said, a simple old song that his wife used to sing while she was cooking. He wanted to be able to play it perfectly on the anniversary of their wedding, in two months’ time.

Can walked back to his flat feeling very different from the man who had knocked on the door. He was not a violinist, but he understood sound better than most people. The next day, he returned with some of his equipment. He showed Ruhi Bey how to record himself, so he could hear his own mistakes more clearly. He suggested a better position for the music stand, near a soft sofa that would absorb some of the sound. They also agreed on a new practice time: ten o’clock instead of eight.

Over the following weeks, the music through the wall slowly improved. The mistakes became less frequent, the long notes became steadier and the song began to sound like a song. Can found that he was actually listening for it in the mornings.

On the anniversary, Ruhi Bey invited Can, his daughter and a few neighbours to his flat. He stood by the window, took a deep breath and played the whole piece without a single mistake. When he finished, nobody clapped for a moment. Then his daughter hugged him, and everyone in the room was smiling, including the sound engineer who had once wanted silence above all else.

questions.q: Why was Ruhi Bey practising the same piece every day?
options: He wanted to play it perfectly on his wedding anniversary.
He was preparing for a concert in Canada.
His teacher gave him homework.
He wanted to annoy his new neighbour.
questions.explain: Ruhi Bey, eşinin söylediği şarkıyı evlilik yıldönümlerinde kusursuz çalmak istiyordu: "He wanted to play it perfectly on his wedding anniversary."

questions.q: How did Can help Ruhi Bey?
options: He gave him violin lessons.
He bought him a new violin.
He showed him how to record himself and improve his practice.
He asked the other neighbours to be quiet.
questions.explain: Can, ses mühendisi olarak ona kendini kaydetmeyi ve çalışmasını iyileştirmeyi gösterdi: "He showed him how to record himself and improve his practice."

title: Two Photographs of a Bridge
text:
Leyla found the photograph inside an old book she had bought for almost nothing at a second-hand market in Izmir. It was a black and white picture of a young couple standing on a stone bridge over a river. The woman was laughing, holding her hat against the wind. On the back, someone had written in faded ink: “Our bridge. Spring 1962. Always.”

Leyla was a photography student, and she was immediately fascinated. Who were these people? Where was the bridge? And why had such a personal photograph ended up in a box of cheap books? She showed it to her friends, but nobody recognised the place. The bridge had three arches, and behind it was a small mosque with a single minaret and a large plane tree.

She decided to find it. For weeks, she spent her free evenings searching online, comparing her photograph with hundreds of pictures of old bridges in western Türkiye. Most of them were too big, too modern or in the wrong kind of landscape. She began to wonder whether the bridge had been destroyed years ago.

Then, one night, she found it. A local history group had posted an old postcard of a small town in the hills. In the corner of the picture was a bridge with three arches, a slim minaret and a huge plane tree. Leyla checked the details again and again. It was the same place.

The following weekend, she took a bus to the town. The bridge was still there, older and greyer, with a few modern repairs. The plane tree was even bigger now. Leyla stood exactly where the couple had stood and took a photograph from the same angle. Then she went into a nearby teahouse and showed the old picture to the owner.

He studied it carefully and called his father from the back room. The old man put on his glasses, looked at the picture and smiled slowly. “That is Nurettin, the pharmacist’s son,” he said. “And that is Melek. They married that summer. Everyone in town came to the wedding.”

Nurettin had died some years earlier, the old man explained, but Melek was still alive. She was now in her eighties and lived with her son in Izmir. After her husband’s death, the family had moved and cleared out the old house. Some boxes of books must have been sold or given away.

With the help of the teahouse owner, Leyla found the family’s phone number. A week later, she sat in a bright flat in Izmir, opposite a small woman with silver hair and the same laugh as the young woman in the picture. Melek held the photograph in both hands for a long time without speaking.

“I thought I had lost this forever,” she said finally. “He wrote those words on the day he asked me to marry him.”

Leyla gave her the old photograph and also the new one she had taken of the bridge. Melek placed them side by side on the table: the same bridge, sixty years apart. For her final project at university, Leyla created an exhibition called “Then and Now”, pairing old photographs with new ones taken from the same places. The first pair, at the entrance, showed a stone bridge, a plane tree and a woman holding her hat against the wind.

questions.q: How did Leyla finally find the bridge?
options: A friend recognised it immediately.
She saw it in an old postcard posted by a local history group.
The teahouse owner sent her the address.
Melek's son contacted her.
questions.explain: Leyla köprüyü yerel bir tarih grubunun paylaştığı eski bir kartpostalda buldu: "She saw it in an old postcard posted by a local history group."

questions.q: What did Leyla give Melek?
options: Only the new photograph of the bridge.
A book about the town's history.
A ticket to her exhibition.
The old photograph and a new one of the same bridge.
questions.explain: Leyla eski fotoğrafı ve köprünün aynı açıdan çektiği yeni fotoğrafını verdi: "The old photograph and a new one of the same bridge."
